CHAPTER III
 
SCHEMES, POLICIES AND PROGRAMMES OF THE MINISTRY
 
Revamping of Civil Defence
8.0       Civil Defence is an important aspect of the country’s internal defence system. In accordance with the Civil Defence Act, 1960, Civil Defence
Corps have been established in the States. National Civil Defence College, Nagpur does the task of professionally training volunteers for Civil Defence. 
The Home Ministry, besides maintaining this institution, has been reimbursing State Governments, in the form of grants-in-aid, some part of the

ONE HUNDRED & NINETEENTH REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/ha/119threport.htm[01-07-2016 11:34:44]
expenditure incurred on the authorized items for raising and training of volunteers, provision of equipment and services, etc for civil defence. On the basis
of the report of Group of Ministers on “Reforming the National Security System” a scheme for revamping of the Civil Defence System in the country was
proposed at an expenditure of Rs. 327.84 crore in 2005-06 for a period of four years.
 
8.1       In accordance with the aforesaid Report, the scheme of ‘Revamping of Civil Defence in States’ was drawn up in 2005-06 with a view to  providing
‘Grants-in-aid’ to the States in a phased manner and  Rs. 50 crore was provided in BE 2005-06.  However, the Ministry have now stated that due to non-
finalization of modalities of the scheme, the amount could not be utilized and no provision was made at the RE stage. In BE 2006-07 there is, however, a
token provision of Rs. 1 lakh for the same.
 
8.2       Explaining the reasons for non-finalization of modalities for such an important scheme for two consecutive years and making only a token
provision of Rs. 1 lakh, the Ministry in the written reply, stated that the detailed scheme for ‘Revamping of Civil Defence’ was formulated for placement
before the Committee on Non-Plan Expenditure. In the meanwhile, the newly constituted National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) desired to
have detailed discussion with the Director General of Civil Defence and Ministry of Home Affairs on the scheme of ‘Revamping of Civil Defence’ in
view of the increasing role of the Civil Defence Organisation in the field of Disaster Management.  A Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri K.M.
Singh, Member, NDMA was set up for this purpose. It was also stated that the recommendations of the Committee were likely to be available soon and
the recast proposal based on the recommendations of the Committee would be placed before the Committee on Non-Plan Expenditure and the Cabinet for
final approval which would take some more time. Hence only a token provision of Rs. 1 lakh has been made in BE 2006-2007. The Ministry further stated
that additional funds, if required, would be sought in the first batch of Supplementary Demands/Revised Estimates for 2006-2007 depending upon the
progress.
 
8.3       Civil Defence is an important and integral part of the defence of the country. Particularly during times of war Civil Defence Organisation has a
vital role in guarding and protecting the people and supporting civil administration. The Committee appreciates that NDMA proposes to have relook at the
scheme of Revamping of Civil Defence and integrate it into the National Disaster Management. The Committee agrees that civil defence is the right
organisation to be involved in Disaster Management.  It however feels that unduly long time has been taken for revamping the Civil Defence System.  The
Committee therefore recommends that the issue may be got cleared from the NDMA Committee and the Non-Plan Expenditure Committee and the final
plan of action may be prepared for revamping the Civil Defence in the shortest possible time schedule. The Committee also recommends that funds for the
scheme may be allocated at RE 2006-07 stage and the scheme may be implemented during the current financial year.
 
Modernization of Fire Services
 
9.0       Preservation of life and property of the people being the States’ responsibility, the State Governments maintain fire services for its prevention and
fighting.  The Ministry of Home Affairs renders technical advice to States/UTs and Central Ministries on Fire Protection, Fire Prevention and Fire
Legislation.  The Government had drawn up a scheme in 2005-06 for Modernisation of Fire Services in the states for a period of five years starting from
2005-06. The scheme was finalised in consultation with the State Governments. The scheme envisaged that the Fire Services would be strengthened by
adding 1856 numbers of fire stations, upgrading existing training centres in stages, providing upgraded versions of water tenders, resume tenders, etc to
augment the existing fleet. A provision of Rs. 134.26 crore was made in BE 2005-06 for Grants-in-aid to States for ‘Modernization of Fire Services’.
However, there was no allocation reflected in RE 2005-06. Similarly only a token provision of Rs. 1 lakh have been made in BE 2006-07 for the purpose
on the ground that modalities of the scheme could not be finalized.
 
9.1       In response to a query of the Committee about the reasons for delay in finalizing the modalities for such an important and critical scheme, the
Ministry stated that an amount of Rs. 134.26 crore in BE 2005-06 was initially provided on Non-Plan side for the scheme for “Modernisation of Fire
Services”. However, at the appraisal and scrutiny stage, the Ministry of Finance advised them that it would be more appropriate to take up the scheme on
Plan side.  Accordingly, the Ministry requested the Planning Commission to provide necessary funds on Plan side to take up the scheme.  The Ministry
further stated that pending adequate provision of funds, a token provision of Rs. 1 lakh was made in BE 2006-07, and action for implementation of the
project would be initiated as soon as funds on the Plan side were provided and project approvals obtained. Clarifying the position further, the AS & FA in
his oral submission stated that last year they had prepared the proposal.  The process of approaching Planning Commission took away a lot of time. The
Home Secretary added that the entire exercise was in progress in consultation with State Governments and NDMA. The Home Secretary also stated that
they intended to come out with the scheme very soon and hence the token provision,
 
9.2       The Committee regrets that as in the case of the scheme of Revamping of Civil Defence, the scheme of Modernisation of Fire Services too could
not take off last year inspite of a provision of Rs. 134.26 crore in BE 2005-06. The Committee takes a serious view of the fact that new schemes are
initiated, allocations are made and they do not take off due to procedural and administrative delays. Although fire services in the country are primarily the
responsibility of the States/Municipal Committees/ Corporations, the services across the country are abysmally below the International Standards. The
Committee desires that Modernisation of Fire services which is a comprehensive scheme should be equipped with modern technology, gadgets and
infrastructure.  The Committee while expressing concern over delay of one year in implementing the scheme urges upon the Government to get the
scheme cleared in a definite time frame from NDMA and Planning Commission and make necessary allocation at RE 2006-07 stage. The Committee also
urges upon the Ministry to implement the scheme during the current fiscal year.
 
Modernisation of Prison Administration
 
10.0     Prison being a State subject under Entry- 4 of List –II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, the responsibility of maintaining
prisons and improving its administration lie mainly with the respective State Governments. However, keeping in view the apathetic approach of the State
Governments in improving their prison system, a ‘Non-Plan’ scheme of ‘Modernisation of Prison Administration’ for a five-year period was launched by
the Ministry in 2002-03 with an outlay of Rs. 1800 crore on cost sharing basis between Centre and the States in the ratio of 75:25. The estimated annual
allocation to all States was Rs. 360 crore out of which  Rs. 270 crore would be the share of Centre and  the remaining Rs 90 crore would be  States’
share.   A sum of Rs. 284 crore was provided in BE 2005-06.   However in the RE 2005-06 and BE 2006-07 it has been reduced sharply to Rs 180 crore.
 
10.1     On being asked about the reason for the sharp reduction in the BE allocation on such an important scheme, the Ministry informed that the Cabinet
approval for the aforesaid scheme was obtained in September 2002.  Subsequently the State Governments were requested to send their perspective plans

and the Annual Action Plan (AAP) for 2002-03.  After the State Governments submitted their plans and these were scrutinized and approved by the
Empowered Committee, the Central share of Rs. 270 crore was released to 27 States at the fag end of 2002-03. Since the funds to the State Governments
were released at the fag end of the financial year 2002-03, they were given 18 months time to complete the work.  Consequently, the funds under AAP
2003-04 were released only in the last quarter of the financial year 2003-04.  Due to initial teething problems such as delay in preparation and approval of
estimates, release of matching share by the State Governments to the implementing agencies, land acquisition etc, there was further delay and the scheme
was virtually behind schedule by almost two years. Hence the utilization of funds was not upto the mark (Rs. 76.05 crores as on 31.3.2004). However,
there was substantial improvement in the utilization of funds during 2005-06, which stood at Rs. 396.4 crores.
 
10.2     The Ministry further apprised the Committee that as per latest reports received, majority of the States have started performing well, some doing
exceedingly well like Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Orissa, Haryana and Uttaranchal. States such as UP, West Bengal, Tamilnadu, Rajasthan, Nagaland,
Mizoram, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Himachal Pradesh too improved their performance. But five States viz. Assam, Bihar, Jharkhand, Kerala and
Punjab have not performed upto the mark.
 
10.3     The Committee was also informed that the releases to the State Governments were made on the basis of their performances.  Due to this reason,
the full Central share could not be released against the annual action plans of 2003-04, 2004-05 and 2005-06 to all States. Since releases to the State
Government were based on their performance, the RE 2005-06 had to be reduced. However, since majority of the States were now performing well, the
Ministry would require more funds in 2006-07 with a view to releasing the shortfall of the amount of pervious years to State Governments as well as the
fund against the AAP 2006-07. It was further added that the Budget Estimate of Rs 180 crore for 2006-07 would be inadequate to meet the requirement
and they were in the process of seeking Cabinet approval for extension of this scheme by a period of two years with effect from 1.4.2007 without affecting
total outlay of Rs. 1800 crore.
 
10.4     The Home Secretary during his oral submission stated that this was one of the thrust areas of the Home Minister and he had addressed letters to all
the Chief Ministers observing that if in the ratio of 75:25 they could not bring the prison modernisation, what the Union Government could do. He further
stated that the Finance Ministry had said that if they could not spend, then that Ministry would be reducing the allocation.  The Home Secretary submitted
that after the States got the message, the expenditure had picked up in the last three months.             
 
10.5     The Committee expresses its serious concern over the laxity of some States in implementing the scheme. Improving the conditions of prisons has
been a widely discussed topic in the public domain.  There is no two opinion that prisons in the country need to be humanized. Infrastructure and living
conditions inside the prisons need to be improved. The present scheme of the Government, if implemented in the right earnest, would go a long way in
improving the conditions, if not completely change the face of the Prisons. The Committee would therefore like the Ministry of Home Affairs to
coordinate closely with the State Governments and impress upon them the need for timely and effective implementation of the Scheme. The Committee
recommends that the additional allocation for the purpose may be made at the RE stage.  The Committee agrees that the scheme needs to be extended for
two years, as desired by the Ministry so that the full amount of Rs.1800 crore is utilised.
 
Bodoland Territorial Council
 
11.0     A Memorandum of Settlement (MoS) was signed between the Central Government, Government of Assam and the Bodo Liberation Tigers (BLT)
on February 10, 2003. As per the Memorandum of Settlement, Government of India are committed to providing Rs. 100 crore per annum on specific
projects to develop the socio-economic infrastructure in Bodoland Territorial Area Districts (BTAD) area for 5 years, over and above the normal plan
assistance to the State of Assam.   With the creation of a full fledged Ministry i.e. Ministry of DoNER on 27 May, 2004 the said provision has been
included in the Ministry of DoNER’s budget.  the allocation to Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) includes the provision of Rs. 100 crore
for Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) for undertaking developmental activities in the Bodo Region. The Ministry has already released Rs. 187 Crore for
the BTC so far and a sum of Rs. 100 Crore has been allocated in the Budget of the Ministry of DoNER in the BE 2006-07.
 
11.1     On being asked to clarify as to why the allocation for Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) was being provided out of the NLCPR and why the
Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) could not make the allocation separately in view of the agreement entered into by them, the AS&FA stated that it must
have been because the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) largely dealt with only non-plan funds.  The Home Secretary added that as a development
ministry for North-East, the Ministry of DoNER dealt with all the plan funding.  He, however, assured that he would have a meeting with the Ministry of
DoNER and review the problem in funding this.
 
11.2     The allocation of Rs. 100 crore made for the development of BTC is a separate package announced by the Government of India as per the
agreement.  But the Committee is not in agreement with the practice of making this provision out of the allocation made to NLCPR. NLCPR being an
accumulation of unspent balance of the 10% earmarked in the Budget by various Ministries/Departments, is primarily a development fund; using it for
other schemes is a negation of the rationale behind the creation of the Fund. NLCPR has a very limited reserve and if this Rs. 100 crore is provided out of
this Fund for BTC, the fund would get depleted.  The Committee feels that the NLCPR being a fund for development of NE States, should be used for the
purpose for which it is created.  The Ministry of Home Affairs may therefore decide on allocation of Rs.100 crore for BTC out of their resources.  
 
Pensionary benefits to CPOs 
12.0     The Central Police Organisations (CPOs) such as Assam Rifles, Border Security Force, Central Reserve Police Force, Indo-Tibetan Border Police,
Central Industrial Security Force, National Security Guard and Sashashtra Seema Bal play an important role in maintaining internal law and order and
guarding the international borders during peace time.  The Central Police Forces (CPFs) are made available in aid of the State Governments to maintain
public order.  These Forces play a key role in the overall management of the internal security situation in the country.  The emerging security scenario has
resulted in increased involvement of CPFs in countering threats of terrorism and militancy.  The Forces have played a major role in helping the State of
Jammu and Kashmir, North-Eastern States and naxal-affected States in combating terrorism/militancy.  They have also assisted in smooth conduct of free,
fair and peaceful Parliamentary and Assembly Elections in the country.  During the recent visit to North-Eastern Region, the Committee was given to
understand that under the New Pension Scheme of the Central Government, the pensionary benefits were discontinued for the Assam Rifles’ personnel
whereas it was available to Army personnel.  On being asked to clarify the position, the Ministry in the written reply stated:

Relief and rehabilitation measures for Kashmiri Migrants
 
13.0     The growth of militancy, the consequential casualties to the civilians in the State of J&K and the resultant migration of the Kashmiri minorities
from the valley in 1990s and thereafter forced the Government to plan for providing relief and rehabilitation to the affected people.  Hence, the Central
Government initiated a policy to provide relief and rehabilitation to the affected families under the Grant-Other Expenditure of MHA.
 
13.1     The allocation under the sub-head ‘Relief & Rehabilitation’  in Demand No. 53 was reduced in RE 2005-06 to Rs.129.80 crore from BE 2005-06
(Rs. 153.11 crore) and the budgetary provision made in BE 2006-07 is Rs. 120 crore.
 
13.2     The Ministry, in the explanatory note to the Demands for Grants, 2006-07, explaining about the reasons for reduction of allocation of RE 2005-06
and BE 2006-07, stated that it was done on the basis of the trend of expenditure. Further, clarifying the position, AS &FA stated that these were basically
reimbursement proposals and the proposals were not forthcoming.  The proposals were not coming from the J& K State in time and this was the main
reason in releasing the funds.
 
13.3     The Committee regrets to observe that the Government is not serious in fully utilising the amount allocated at BE stage for rehabilitation of J & K
migrants. When Central Government has made the allocation, State like J & K should have come forward with the schemes for utilising the money,
particularly in view of its being a terrorist savaged State. The Committee further observes that the State Government should not have any hesitation in
formulating the schemes for which Central Government is prepared to allocate necessary funds.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation
made in its 112
th Report (para 8.3, page 15) on Demands for Grants (2005-06) that the full amount allocated for the rehabilitation schemes for the J&K
migrants should be utilised. The Committee also urges upon the Government to impress upon the J & K Government to come forward with schemes in
time and implement them without delay.
 
Multipurpose National Identity Card Scheme
 
14.0     The Government has been contemplating to prepare a National Register of Indian Citizens and issue Multipurpose National Identity Cards
(MNICs) to all the citizens. A pilot project covering certain districts of twelve States and one Union Territory (Pondicherry) was initiated in November
2003, envisaging preparation of Centralised Population Register, allocation of a unique identity number, issuance of National Identity Card, maintenance
of the register for at least one year and also for providing other MNIC related services for a period of one year.  The project was expected to be completed
by April 2005. However, it has not been completed as yet and the Ministry has informed that a decision on production and distribution of cards in the pilot
project was to be made shortly and that after the award of work it would take another 6-7 months in completing the project.  
 
14.1     Replying to a query regarding the time schedule for completing the National Register of Citizens and issuing of MNICs to all the citizens of the
country, the Ministry in the written reply stated that the pilot project on MNIC had brought out the complexities involved both in regard to the processes
as well as technology issues, and the technology issues in regard to data retrieval, data warehousing and data management were yet to be tried and tested. 
The logistic and operational requirements for the national rollout were going to be enormous, the Ministry stated.  It was further stated that to optimize the
cost of implementation, this would have to be done synchronously with other schemes of the Government, and all these issues were being addressed and a
comprehensive proposal on the methodology as well as timing of the national roll-out was under preparation.
 
14.2     ‘The importance of the Mulit-purpose National Identity Card Scheme         (MNICs) in a country like India with thousands of kilometres  of porous
International Border and with the large presence of illegal immigrants posing a grave threat to the internal security, need not be overemphasized.  The
Committee is, however, disappointed at the pace of implementation of the pilot project.  If the pilot project itself is taking such a long time, preparation of
MNICs for all the citizens may take several more years.  The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Government to accord high priority to the Scheme and
accelerate completion of the Pilot Project within a specific time frame rather than dragging it endlessly.  The Committee is confident that based on the
experience gathered in the implementation of the Pilot Scheme for the last two and a half years, the government would be in a position to evolve time
bound action plan for implementation of the scheme at the national level’.
 
Naxalism
 
15.0     As per available information, the present strength of armed naxalite cadres is around 7200. Naxal violence was reported from 509 police stations in
2005 as against 517 in 2004 and 518 in 2003. Overall, parts of 76 districts in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Chhattisgarh, Bihar Jharkhand,
Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Maharastra and West Bengal, though in varying degrees, have been badly affected by naxal violence.  Naxals have,
however, been trying to increase their influence and activity in parts of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and Uttaranchal. These States are also sensitized
from time to time to stop such naxal activities right at the initial stage. The Union Home Minister while submitting the Demands for Grants (2006-07) of

through Development’.  They are reportedly digging wells, developing land, cultivation, education, etc.   An informal tax system is also allegedly being

15.3     The Ministry reacting to these developments stated that the Central Government view the naxalite menace as a matter of serious concern.  A multi-

economic development and redress legitimate grievances of the people in these areas.  Specific measures were taken to coordinate and supplement the

15.4     Further replying about the initiatives in the direction of socio-economic upliftment of the masses in the naxal affected regions as a measure to
combat naxalism, the Ministry stated that the Government adopted a multi-pronged approach to combat the naxal problem which, inter-alia,  included
focussed attention on integrated socio-economic development in the naxal affected areas.  Besides, various Centrally Sponsored Schemes meant to
provide funds to the States for socio-economic development, the Central government has sanctioned Rs. 2475 crore under the Backward District Initiative
(BDI) component of the Rashtriya Sam Vikas Yojana (RSVY) to fill in the critical gaps in social and physical infrastructure in the naxal affected districts.
 
15.5     The Committee expresses its serious concern over the growing influence of naxalites all over the country and feels that it is no more a law and

Modernization of police force
 
16.0     Modernization of police force is an ongoing process which enables Police Forces to keep pace with the changing security scenario.  In the light of
the challenges being faced by the police forces, the necessity of modernization  gains momentum. The Ministry of Home Affairs has been implementing a
Non-plan Scheme for Modernization of State Police forces since 1969-70 to supplement the efforts of the State Governments in modernizing their police
forces. The Scheme provided assistance to the State Governments on 50 per cent  “Grants-in-Aid” and 50 per cent loan basis.  In view of the changing
situation of internal security in the country, the annual Central assistance under the scheme was pegged at Rs. 1000 crore in 2000-01 which was further
enhanced to Ra. 1400 crore from 2003-04. While enhancing the annual Central allocation during 2003-04, it was also decided to give the Central
assistance only as “Grants-in-Aid”.
 
16.1     The Ministry, in its written reply, stated that the scheme made  perceptible impact, as proper buildings for  police stations/outposts taken up under
the Scheme has provided safe and secure environment, construction of houses for police personnel and provision of modern weaponry have boosted their
morale.   
 
16.2     On being asked to clarify as to why the scheme of modernisation of police force was not being implemented in UTs even though it was
implemented in the States, the Home Secretary stated that the Ministry of Finance felt that since the funding of the UT was done by the Ministry of Home
Affairs, the modernisation aspect should not be a part of this scheme and the UT allocation may be increased rather than dovetailing with the Police
Organizations. 
 
16.3     In this regard, the Home Secretary, while deposing before the Committee stated that Ministry of Home Affairs had planned to introduce a separate
Police Modernization Scheme for the Union Territories including Delhi allocating Rs. 884 crores for a period of five yeas starting from 2006-07 but it
could not be included in the BE 2006-07 as the approval of the Cabinet was received in February 2005.
 
16.4     The Committee is constrained to learn that the scheme of such a magnitude and importance has not been implemented in the Union Territories
though it has been  implemented in the States.   The Committee feels that the scheme  should have been taken up on a priority basis and the proposed
allocation could have been made a part of the budgetary provision of 2006-07, if the necessary processing was done well in time.  The Committee hopes
that necessary allocation would be made at RE stage in 2006-07 and the scheme would take off in the current financial year.

Delhi Police
 
17.0     Being the Police of the National Capital Territory, expectations of the people from Delhi Police always remain very high.  The heterogeneous
nature of the NCT’s population with large scale migration which is 3 to 3.5 lakhs every year from neighbouring as well as other States, makes the task of
its Police more arduous and challenging.  While providing Legislature to Delhi, one of the two subjects kept by the Central Government within its
jurisdiction is law and order which is in effect means, Delhi Police.  Though growth of crime is a natural phenomenon, but increase in population of the
city of about five lakhs (3 to 3.5 lakhs migrants, 1.5 to 2.0 lakhs natural growth) each year stretches the manpower of the force to the maximum.
 
17.1     While making oral presentation before the Committee on 26 April 2006 the Commissioner of Police reiterated the commitment of Delhi Police to
strive for excellence and to remain focussed on most of the nagging problems.    He emphasized to make Delhi Police a first rate service organization.  
 
17.2     According to him all these initiatives have brought down the number of complaints against the police and also the number of strictures from courts.
He also contended that response time of PCR had improved, and in the last few months though Delhi Police had been over stretched on account of slum
clearance, demolitions and sealing drive, but these activities had no adverse impact on the law and order situation.  Conviction rate has also improved 
from 50.29% in 2004 to 55% in 2005.
 
17.3     On being asked to comment on the negative image of police among the people, the Commissioner of Police stated that working of police and its
behaviour to people was improving, and the number of complaints from the public, cases of human rights violations have decreased.
 
17.4     He also stated that Delhi Police was trying hard to wipe out the negative image by reaching out to the people and working in a transparent manner.
 
17.5     The Committee while appreciating the efforts being made by Delhi Police to improve its functioning and also to improve its image, feels that there
is still a lot of room for improvement.  The Committee recommends that Delhi Police should conduct a survey on the perception of the people about it.  
Senior officers should undertake surprise and disguised visits to police stations and deploy decoy complainants and observe the behaviour of the personnel
there.  It will give Delhi Police important inputs about effectiveness of its various steps at the ground level, trying to improve its functioning and its
interface with the public. 
 
Crime Against Women
 
17.6     Intensity and dimension of crime against women is a cause of serious concern.  It has instilled in them a sense of fear and panic, cutting across the
age profile.  Women being vulnerable, they fall easy prey to criminals and anti-social elements. Amongst the victims of crime, women are the worst hit
group.  As per the information furnished to the Committee by the Ministry of Home Affairs rape cases have been increasing every year from 2001 to
2005. It witnessed 20% increase in 2005 over the previous year. It is heading towards an alarming situation.  Murder of elderly women staying alone is
another serious dimension of crime against them. Keeping in view the scenario prevailing in the city, women do not feel safe and secured. 
17.7     Addressing the concern of the Committee about crime against women, the Commissioner of Police in his oral submission before it stated that the
number of rape cases had shown a declining trend and had already come down by over 20 per cent during first 3-4 months of the year 2006 and 97.5%
cases of rape were committed by known acquaintances and only 2.5% rapes cases were reported to be done by strangers. 
 
17.8     When the Commissioner, Delhi Police was asked about the plans to have all women police station in Delhi, he responded that this issue had been
examined in great detail.  Keeping in view, the location and compactness of the city, having all women police station would not be that advantageous.
 
17.9     He further stated that Delhi Police had a Crime Against Women Cell in Nanakpura at Central level, besides Crime Against Women Cell in all
district headquarters.  At the Reception Desk of each police station, there was a women receptionist.  Woman Police were deployed at places which were
sensitive and where women have more interaction and are work vulnerable, the Commissioner of Police stated. 
 
17.10.0            The way crime is perpetrated against women in Delhi and the feeling that women are not safe and secure in the National Capital Region do
not give a positive picture about the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi to the rest of the world. This perception will have a negative impact on the
women tourists visiting India.  The Committee feels that the crime against women seems to have acquired serious proportions and is anguished to note
that all efforts made in this regard by Delhi Police have failed to bring substantial change in the situation.  It is legally as well as morally binding upon the
law enforcement agency to make sincere efforts in nabbing the perpetrators of crime against women and see to it that punishment is handed down in such
a way as to set an example to deter potential offenders.  The Committee is of the view that the lackluster style of functioning of the police force is greatly
responsible for not instilling a sense of security and confidence amongst the women in Delhi. The Committee, therefore, recommends that adequate
women police personnel should be deployed in police stations and at other places considered vulnerable for women. Investigation of cases of crime
against women should be completed within a definite time frame so that conviction of the delinquent is secured without losing time. The Committee also
recommends that Delhi Police should launch a drive to educate women in self-defence through posters and pamphlets and also launch awareness
campaigns amongst women about their proactive approach in dealing with the cases of atrocities committed against them.   The Committee further
recommends that Delhi Police should address this issue with utmost sincerity and honesty by adopting all necessary measures.  
 
17.10.1            The Committee is also given to understand that a large number of women are working in Call Centers in NCR and travel long distance
from their place of residence to their place of work at odd hours.  Cases of rapes and atrocities on such women employees have been reported from certain
places.  The Committee, therefore, desires that Delhi Police should take all precautionary measures to ensure that such incidents do not happen in NCT of
Delhi. The Committee also feels that there is a need for gender sensitization among Delhi Police personnel and all efforts may be made for ensuring
attitudinal change amongst Delhi Police personnel.

vital role in guarding and protecting the people and supporting civil administration. The Committee appreciates that NDMA proposes to have relook at the

there.  It will give Delhi Police important inputs about effectiveness of its various steps at the ground level, trying to improve its functioning and its
interface with the public.                                                                                                                               (para 17.5)
 
Crime Against Women

ONE HUNDRED & NINETEENTH REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/ha/119threport.htm[01-07-2016 11:34:44]
 
The way crime is perpetrated against women in Delhi and the feeling that women are not safe and secure in the National Capital Region do not
give a positive picture about the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi to the rest of the world. This perception will have a negative impact on the
women tourists visiting India.  The Committee feels that the crime against women seems to have acquired serious proportions and is anguished to note
that all efforts made in this regard by Delhi Police have failed to bring substantial change in the situation.  It is legally as well as morally binding upon the
law enforcement agency to make sincere efforts in nabbing the perpetrators of crime against women and see to it that punishment is handed down in such
a way as to set an example to deter potential offenders.  The Committee is of the view that the lackluster style of functioning of the police force is greatly
responsible for not instilling a sense of security and confidence amongst the women in Delhi. The Committee, therefore, recommends that adequate
women police personnel should be deployed in police stations and at other places considered vulnerable for women. Investigation of cases of crime
against women should be completed within a definite time frame so that conviction of the delinquent is secured without losing time. The Committee also
recommends that Delhi Police should launch a drive to educate women in self-defence through posters and pamphlets and also launch awareness
campaigns amongst women about their proactive approach in dealing with the cases of atrocities committed against them.   The Committee further
recommends that Delhi Police should address this issue with utmost sincerity and honesty by adopting all necessary measures.       
                                                                   (para 17.10.0)
 
The Committee is also given to understand that a large number of women are working in Call Centers in NCR and travel long distance from their
place of residence to their place of work at odd hours.  Cases of rapes and atrocities on such women employees have been reported from certain places. 
The Committee, therefore, desires that Delhi Police should take all precautionary measures to ensure that such incidents do not happen in NCT of Delhi.
The Committee also feels that there is a need for gender sensitization among Delhi Police personnel and all efforts may be made for ensuring attitudinal
change amongst Delhi Police personnel.             (para 17.10.1)
 
Housing
 
The Committee feels that proper housing facilities for police personnel particularly at the level of Constable and Head Constable will go a long
way in improving their efficiency particularly their attitude and behaviour.  The Committee expresses its deep anguish over the laxity shown by Delhi
Police in improving the satisfaction level in the housing of Delhi Police personnel particularly at lower level.  Inspite of serious concern expressed by the
Committee in the earlier years and recommendations made for improvement, there is no perceptible change in the situation.  Housing is one of the basic
requirements, particularly for people working in an organisation like Delhi Police and it should be made available to the extent possible.  The Committee
also expresses its concern that inspite of facing problem from several fronts in meeting the housing requirement they have not been able to set up the Delhi
Police Housing Corporation.  Housing Corporation will be an important step in the direction of solving the problem and the Committee strongly
recommends that it may be established during the current financial year. The allocation made for housing in the current year i.e. Rs.55 crore may be fully
utilized in the construction and purchase of housing units.  The Committee is happy to learn that Rs. 100 crore are going to be made available every year
for housing of Delhi Police personnel from out of the new scheme likely to be launched i.e. Modernisation of Police Forces in UTs.  The allocation could
not be made for this scheme at BE 2006-07 due to procedural delay and the Committee has already made its observation in para 16.4 supra.            Since
the scheme has already been approved, the Committee desires that allocation may be made for the scheme and Delhi Police may finalise its proposal for
utilisation  of the amount likely to be made available to it.                                                                                                                                 (para 17.14)

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorized 
by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, present this Twelfth report of 
the Committee relating to the Representation of the People (Second Amendment) 
Bill*, 1994. The Bill seeks to amend the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and 
the Representation of the People Act, 1951. 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker, 
Lok Sabha referred** the Bill, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 13th June, 
1994, and pending in that House, to the Committee for examination and report. 
3. The Committee held 13 sittings in all. In its sitting held on the 18th July, 
~ 
1994, the Committee held preliminary discussions on the Bill and also discussed the 
procedure to be followed by it in regard thereto. The Committee decided that a press 
release inviting views, suggestions and comments from interested individuals, 
institutions, etc. be issued. A copy of the press release is placed at Annexure - I. 
4. In response to the press release, 25 memoranda containing views, suggestions 
etc. on the various provisions of the Bill were received by the Committee. A list of 
individuals etc. from whom memoranda were received is placed at Annexure - II. 
5. The Committee heard the views of various eminent persons. It also heard the 
Law Secretary in the matter. A list of such persons is placed at Annexure - III. 
6. In its sittings held on the 17th, 18th, 19th, 26th and 27th October, 1994, the 
Committee had clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill. 
7. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its sitting held on the 
16th November, 1994. 
8. The Committee considered the various papers and memoranda placed before it 
and also the views expressed by the witnesses on the Bill. It also considered the 
viewpoints put forth by the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs.

9. The Committee makes the following recommendations/observations on the Bill:-
CLAUSES 2 & 3 
The Committee discussed these clauses at length. In this context, it also 
considered the situation that could arise in view of the Election Commission's letter 
dated the 28th August, 1993 addressed to the Chief Electoral Officers and the Chief 
Secretaries of all States/Union Territories (except Jammu and Kashmir) that no 
elections would be held in 543 parliamentary constituencies throughout the country 
after 1st January, 1995 unless all eligible electors were supplied with Identity Cards. 
In this connection, the Committee noted that on the one hand every citizen of this 
country had a right to vote as guaranteed by the Constitution, on the other it was 
the Executive which had to decide when the elections were to be held and the will 
of the Executive was reflected in the notifications issued by the President for Lok 
Sabha and the Governors for State Legislative Assemblies. In these circumstances, it 
could lead to a national crisis if the elections were withheld just on the ground of 
identity cards. It was the general feeling of the members that though identity cards 
were necessary and should be provided to all electors as expeditiously as possible, if 
in a given time frame that process was not completed due to administrative and 
practical difficulties, it would not at all be desirable that elections should be 
withheld. 
Be that as it may, the consensus is in favour of retention of the existing 
provisions. 
CLAUSES 
The Committee agrees with the provtston in the clause. It, however, feels that 
the National Song 'Vande Mataram' enjoys the same status as that of the National 
Anthem 'Jana Gana Mana'. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government 
should consider amending the Prevention of the Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 
to include the National Song also in the Act. 
CLAUSES 7 & 8 
These clauses relate to registration and deregistration of political parties. Some 
members felt that these should be deleted as they would not serve any useful 
purpose and on the other hand, they are likely to create more complications in 
practice. The consensus is, however, to retain these clauses. 
The Committee is of the view that feelings of enmity, hatred or disharmony 
between different classes of citizens can be promoted not only on grounds of religion 
but also many. other factors such as race, caste, creed, sex, community, language or 
place of birth etc. The Committee, therefore, has the consensus that all these factors 
should also be included in clause 8(c). 
2 

The Committee also feels that 'religion' has a wide connotation and is capable 
of being interpreted differently in the absence of any specific definition or 
clarification. It, therefore, suggests that this word needs to be amplified by way of 
an Explanation under Clause 7 or under the definition clause of the Representation 
of the People Act, 1951. 
CLAUSE 10 
The clause seeks to restrict the nomination of a person as a candidate for 
election in more than two constituencies of the same class. 
Whereas some ·members are in favour of retaining the proposed proVISion, the 
Committee finds no justification for permitting nomination of a person as a candidate 
for election to two constituencies of the same class. It, therefore, recommends that 
the nomination be restricted to only one constituency of the same class. 
CLAUSE 13 
The Committee is of the view that the time-limit of seven days to run from 
the date of death of the candidate, proposed in sub-clause (2) for nomination of 
another candidate by a recognised political party in case of death of the earlier 
candidate is not realistic. It, therefore, recommends that the time-limit of seven days 
in this regard be reckoned from the date when the Election Commission calls upon a 
recognised political party to nominate another candidate. 
The Committee finds that the expression 'recognised political party' is 
occuring in more than one clause of the Bill. It is, therefore, of the view that this 
expression can more appropriately be put in the definition clause of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1951. 
CLAUSE 15 
This clause seeks to give statutory backing to certain provlSlons of Part VII 
of the Model Code of Conduct issued by the Election Commission for the guidance 
of political parties and candidates. 
Some members pointed out that the provtston, namely 'use of Government 
transport including official aircraft, vehicles, machinery and personnel for 
electioneering work' mentioned in the Model Code has not been included as an 
illegal practice under the clause. The Law Secretary clarified that the said provision 
had been omitted because of security perceptions relating to various public 
functionaries, which included the Prime Minister, the Home Minister and the Chief 
Ministers. 
The Committee is conscious of the fact that the security consideration of 
various public functionaries is of paramount importance ·and should in no case be 
3 

compromised. It, therefore, leaves to the Government to examine in depth the 
inclusion or otherwi se of the provision as one of the illegal practices taking into 
consideration the views expressed by the members and the security perceptions 
relating to the public functionaries. 
With regard to the wording of the clause, the Committee suggests that the 
word 'indulge' and the words 'in the following practices' may be substituted by the 
'commit' and the words 'any of the following practices', respectively. 
CLAUSE 16 
The Committee feels that the expression 'election matter' defined in sub-clause 
(3) can more appropriately be given by way of an Explanation under sub-clause (2) 
and recommends accordingly. 
ClAUSE 22 
The Committee feels that the proposed punishment in sub-clause (3) is not 
adequate. It, therefore, suggests that the punishment under the sub-clause should be

Under the proposed provision, an elector shall. not be granted a paid holiday 
on the day of poll in case his absence is likely to cause danger and substantial loss 
in respect of the employment in which he is engaged. The Committee feels that the 
proposed provision may interfere with the 'right to vote' of such an elector as he is 
required to attend to his work due to unavoidable circumstances/grounds mentioned in

The Committee, therefore, recommends that suitable mechanism needs to be 
evolved in this regard so that such an elector is not deprived of his 'right to vote'.

Under the proposed provision of Section 135 (C), no spirituous, fermented or

The Committee is not inclined to agree with the views of the Ministry of

NOTE GIVEN BY SHRI MADAN BHATIA, MP 
As a member of the Committee on Horne Affairs, I am in complete 
agreement with the Report on the Representation of the People (Second Amendment) 
Bill, 1994, as submitted by the Hon'ble Chairman of the Committee on its behalf. I 
am writing this note in order to deal with certain legal issues involved in clauses 3, 
7, & 8 of the bill and dispel any misconception about those clauses. I am also 
taking liberty to refer to some aspects which, in my opinion, are covered by the 
intendment of those clauses, but do not form part of the same and may therefore 
need consideration. 
CLAUSE 3 
Clause 3 of the Bill does not in any manner impinge upon the constitutional 
power of the Election Commission under Article 324 of the Constitution of India. 
Nor does it curtail any power of the Election Commission to direct the issue of 
identity cards under the Representation Ol the People Act, 1951 or the Representation 
of the People Act, 1950. It is the Central\oovernment which conferred power on the 
Election Commission to give such directions in the exercise of its rule making power 
under section 28 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. 
It is the Central Government which framed Rule 28 of the Registration of 
Electors Rules 1961 in consultation with the Election Commission, as provided by 
section 28 of ,the Representation of the People Act, 1950, authorizing the Election 
Commission to issue notification for any constituency directing the Registration 
Officer to arrange for the issue of identity cards to electors of that constituency for 
preventing personation. It is from Rule 28 framed by the Central Government that 
the Election Commission derives its existing authority to direct the issue of identity 
cards. 
In fact, prior to 1958 the only proviSIOn which was made in the 
Representation of the People Act, 1951 to prevent personation was for the marking 
with indelible ink of the thumb or any other finger of elector. There was no power 
given to the polling officer to call upon elector to produce any identity card. It was 
in 1958 that the Representation of the People Act, 1951 was amended and such 
. power was given to the polling officer. but only in the event of any rules having 
been framed for supply of identity cards to electors under the Representation of the 
People Act, 1950 and if the cards had been so supplied. In other words, if no such 
rules were framed by the Central Government, there would be no identity cards and 
no power with the polling officer to call upon electors to produce such cards. power 
to frame rules under section 28 of the Representation of the People act, 1950 vests 
in the Central Government alone, to be exercised by it in consultation with the 
Election Commission. Under section 28, the Central Government had the discretion to 
7 

frame rules for issue of identity cards and empower itself to give directions in this 
regard or vest such authority in any other person, including the Election Commission. 
The Central Government, in its wisdom, framed rule 28 empowering the Election 
Commission to issue notification for any constituency for applicability of that rule to 
the same, whereupon it would become incumbent upon the Registration Officer to 
arrange for the issue of identity cards to electors of that constituency. 
But for rule 28 of the Registration of Electors Rules framed by the Central 
Government under section 28 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and in 
view of the specific provisions of section 61(2) of the Representation of the People 
Act, 1951, the Election Commission would have no power to direct the issue of 
identity cards. Article 324 of the Constitution of India does not confer power on the 
Election Commission to transgress or supplant any Act of Parliament or any rule 
framed thereunder. 
The scope and ambit of Article 324 of the Constitution has been considered 
by the Supreme Court in a number of cases culminating in A. C. Jose Vs. Sivan 
Pillai reported in AIR 1984 SC 921. In that case the notification issued by the 
Election Commission for casting votes by means of electronic machines in a 
constituency in Kerala and the · consequent election were challenged by a defeated 
candidate on the ground that the notification of the Election Commission providing 
for use of electronic machines for casting votes was contrary to the provisions of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1951 and the rules framed thereunder. This 
challenge was upheld by the Supreme Court. Both the notification and the voting in 
the polling stations where the voting machines had been used were set aside and a 
repoll in those stations was ordered. The law relating to the power of the Election 
Commission under Article 324 of the Constitution was summed up as follows : -
"a) Where there is no Parliamentary legislation or rule made under the said 
legislation, the Commission is free to pass any order in respect of the 
conduct of elections. 
b) Where there is an Act and express rules made thereunder, it is not open 
to the Commission to override the Act or the rules and pass orders in 
direct disobedience to the mandate contained in the Act or the rules. In 
other words, the powers of the Commission are meant to supplement 
rather than supplant the law (both statute and rules) in the matter of 
superintendencce, direction and control as provided by Article 324; 
c) Where the Act or the rules are silent, the C·:;mmission has no doubt 
plenary power under Article 324 to give any direction in respect of the 
conduct of election; and 
8 

d) Where a particular direction by the Commission is submitted to the 
Government for approval, as required by the rules, it is not open to the 
Commission to go ahead with the implementation of it at its sweet will 
even if the approval of the Government is not given." 
It may be mentioned that prior to the issue of the notification for use 
of the voting machines, the Commission had sought the sanction of the 
Government of India which was, however, refused. 
The Supreme Court further observed, "It is true that Article 324 does 
authorize the Commission to exercise power of superintendence, direction and 
control of prepar:ation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections to 
Parliament and State Legislatures, but then the article has to be read 
harmoniously with the articles that follow and the powers that are given to 
the legislatures under Entry No. 72 in the Union List and Entry No. 37 of 
the State List of the VII Schedule to the Constitution." 
Entry No. 72 of the Union List confers power on the Parliament to make 
laws relating to "elections to Parliament, all the legislatures of the States and to the 
Offices of the President and Vice President; the Election Commission." 
In another part of the same judgement, the Supreme Court further observed, 
"The Commission in the garb of passing orders for regulating the conduct of 
elections cannot take upon itself a purely legislative activity which has been reserved 
under the scheme of the Constitution only to Parliament and the State legislatures." 
The argument raised on behalf of the Commission was that Article 324 was 
the code in itself and was couched in a very plain and simple language which 
admitted of no ambiguity, and if so construed, it gave full power and authority to 
the Commission to give any direction in connection with the conduct of elections. 
This argument was stoutly rejected by the Supreme Court with the following 
strong observations : -
"If we were to accept the contention of the respondent, it would convert the 
Commission into an absolute despot in the field of election so as to give 
directions regarding the mode and manner of elections bypassing the provisions 
of the Act and the rules purporting to exercise power under cover of Article 
324. If the Commission is armed with such unlimited and arbitrary powers 
and if it ever happens, that the person manning the Commission shares or is 
wedded to particular ideology, he could by giving odd directions cause a 
political havoc or bring about a constitutional crisis, setting at naught the 
9 

integrity and independence of the electoral process, so important and 
indispensable to the democratic system." 
The proposed clause 3 puts the matter of issue of identity cards beyond the 
pale of the rule making power of the Central Government whkh carries with it, by 
virtue of section 22 of the General Clauses Act, power to modify or rescind any 
rule. It seeks to vest the power and initiative to direct issue of identity cards in the 
Election Commission through an Act of Parliament, to be exercised by it with the 
previous approval of the Central Government. As at present, the Election Commission 
derives its authority in this regard from the Rule made by the Central Government. 
On the enactment of Clause 3, the Election Commission will derive its authority 
from the Act of Parliament, to be exercised by it with the previous approval of the 
Central Government. The Central Government cannot withhold its approval arbitrarily. 
As held by the Supreme Court in a recent case, "Conferment of the power together 
with the discretion which goes with it to enable exercise of the power is coupled 
with the duty to shun arbitrariness in its exercise and to promote the objects for 
which the power is conferred." 
It is, however, in the fitness of things that there should be prior approval of 
the Central Government. The Election Commission is concerned solely with one 
function, namely conduct of elections. The perspective of the Election Commission is, 
therefore, confined to that function. The representatives of the people in Parliament 
and their elected Government, on the other hand, are concerned with much broader 
perspective, involving multifarious needs, requirements and ground realities of the 
nation, and they have to adjust its priorities accordingly, particularly when the 
resource crunch is being felt in this country in every area of national life as 
demands for higher allocations are coming up from all sections, including the social 
sectors. 
The Central Government has no power to amend Rule 28 retrospectively so as 
to nullify any existing notification already issued thereunder. That apart, as the issue 
of identity cards to electors has become a matter of momentous national importance, 
it was equally appropriate that it should have been resolved by the representatives of 
the people in Parliament on the basis of broad political consensus. Clause 3 of the 
Bill seeks to achieve that objective. 
When clause 3 is enacted, the aforesaid Rule 28 shall stand repealed to the 
extend of inconsistency. If any statute is enacted which is inconsistent with the 
existing law, the existing law stands repealed by virtue of the doctrine of implied 
repeal. The Courts, however, tend to lean against implied repeal by resort to another 
doctrine, namely the doctrine of harmonious construction. Therefore, to avoid any 
judicial controversy, it needs to be considered whether specific provision should not 
10 

be made in clause 3 specifically declaring Rule 28 void and inoperative. 
Clause 3 has been necessitated by the declaration of the Election Commission 
that there shall be no elections in t 995 unless the identity cards have been issued. I 
may, however, state that there is nothing in clause 3 which bars the Election 
Commission from taking such stand if he still chooses to do so after clause 3 is 
enacted. At the same time, there is no specific provision in the Representation of the 
People Act, 1951 which empowers the Election Commission to say that there shall 
be no election unless identity cards are issued to electors. However, under section 14 
of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 in the case of general election for the 
House of the People, the President can issue notification only on such date as may 
be recommended by the Election Commission calling upon parliamentary 
constituencies to elect members. Similar is the circumscribed power of Governors in 
the case of state legislatures. The Election Commission, therefore, can prevent the 
President or the Governor from issuing notification for elections even when the 
durauon of the House of the People or of a state legislature is expiring under the 
Constitution of India, by refusing to recommend any date. 
It therefore needs to be considered whether sections 14 and 15 of the 
Representation of the People Act" ~hould be amended to provide guidelines for the 
exercise of the recommendmg power of the Election Commission and in the case of 
election to the House of the People or a state legislature necessitated by the 
impending expiry of its duration, outer time limit should be provided for the issue of 
the notification making it incumbent for the Election Commission to recommend date 
before the expiry of outer time limit. 
The Election Commission may be given discretion not to recommend date 
before the expiry of the outer time limit in specified circumstances, such as for 
instance, if he is satisfied that on ground of wa:r, internal disturbances, civil strife, 
natural calamity or such like circumstances or even non completion of revision of 
electoral rolls it is not possible to hold elections after the expiry of the outer time 
limit and before the expiry of the constitutional duration of the House of the People 
or the state legislature concerned. 
The following observations of the Supreme Court in Election Commission of 
India Vs. State of Haryana , will be relevant in this regard 
"The Governor of ~aryana is undoubtedly in the best position to assess the 
situation of law and order in areas within his jurisdiction and under his 
control. But the ultimate decision as to whether it is possible and expedient to 
hold the election at any give point of time must rest with the Election 
Commission. It is not suggested that the Election Commission can exercise its 
11 

discretion in an arbitrary or malafide manner. Arbitrariness and malafides 
destroy the validity and efficacy of all orders passed by public authorities." 
"On an important issue such as the holding of election which is of great and 
Immediate concern to the entire political community, there can no question of 
any public official standing on prestige, an apprehension which was faintly 
projected in the state's argument. A sense of realism, objectivity and non­
alignment must inform the decision of the Election Commission on that issue." 
CLAUSE 7 
Clause 7 seeks to substitute the existing proviso of sub-section 7 of section 
29 (A) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. 
Sub-clause (a) of the substituted proviso provides that no association or body 
shall be registered as a political party if it bears a "religious name." More than 
quarter of a century ago, the Supreme Court observed in Kultar Singh V. Mukhtiar 
Singh case decided in 1965, as follows : -
" It is well known that there are several partie s in the country which subscribe 
to different political and economic ideologies, but the membership of them is 
either confined to or predominantly held by members of particular community 
or religion. So long as law does not prohibit the formation of such parties 
and in fact recognises them for the purpose of election and parliamentary 
life, it would be necessary to remember that an appeal made by candidates of 
such parties for votes may, if successful, lead to their election and in an 
indirect way may conceivably be influenced by considerations of religion, race, 
caste, community or language. This infirmity perhaps cannot be avoided so 
long as parties are allowed to function and are recognised when their 
composition may be predominantly based on membership of particular 
community or religion." 
The aforesaid proposed amendment for the first time seeks to grapple with the 
above infirmity pointed our by the Supreme Court. For the membership of a party, 
which carries a religious name, is bound to be confined or predominantly confined to 
members of the religion whose name it bears. 
It, however, needs consideration what other legislative measures can be 
prescribed to eradicate altogether the evil infirmity pointed out by the Supreme 
Court. 
1, may, however, add, that the expression "religious name" is capable of 
restrictive interpretation. 'Religious' can also mean "of religion". In that case 
12 

.. religious name" can be interpreted to mean "name of a religion" and it can be 
argued whether, for example, the word "Muslim" or "Christian" or "Hindu" or 
"Ram" is the name of a religion. 
CLAUSE 8 
Clause (c) of the proposed section 29 B has not come too soon. It has been 
held in recent decisions of the various American Courts that political parties are an 
instrumentality of the State by which the will of the people may be made vocal. In 
American Jurisprudence (Volume 25 under Charter Election) it has been stated as 
follows :-
"Political parties are institution of very great importance under our form of 
Government. They are, in fact, the effective instrumentality by which the will 
of the people may be made vocal and the enactment of laws in accordance 
therewith made possible. So potent they have become in determining the 
measures and in administering the affairs of Government that they are now 
regarded as inseparable from, if not essential to, a republican form of 
government. 
Although earlier decisions held that political parties were completely regulated 
by their party byelaws and constitution, and were not to be regarded as 
constituting a governmental agency or instrumentality, throughout the years 
there has been a marked change in the attitude of the courts towards political 
parties and their primaries, and later decisions indicate that political parties 
have come to be regarded by the courts as governmental agencies through 
which the sovereign power is exercised by the people". 
The Supreme Court has veered round to this view in S.R. Bommai's case' 
(relating to dismissal of certain State Governments). In separate speeches Mr. Justice 
K. Ramaswamy and Mr. Justice Jeevan Reddy have held that a political party which 
is formed and exists to capture or share state power and seeks to accomplish success 
at an election for governance of parliamentary form of Government, is bound by the 
Constitution of India, articles 14, 15, 25 enshrined therein, the basic structure of the 
Constitution, the directive principles and the fundamental duties of citizens contained 
in chapter IV A of the Constitution. 
Mr. Justice K. Ramaswamy held, "For a political party or an organisation that 
seeks to influence the electorates to promote or accomplishing success at an election 
for governance of parliamentary form of Government, the principles are those 
embedded in the Directive Principles of the Constitution vis-a.,vis the Fundamental 
Rights and the Fundamental Duties in part IV A and should abide by the 
Constitution and promote tolerance, harmony and the spirit of commonness amongst 
13 

all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic. regional or sectional 
diversities and to preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture, to develop 
humanism, spirit of reformation and to abstain from violence. Therefore, the 
manifesto of a political party should be consistent with these fundamental and basic 
features of the Constitution, secularism, socio-economic anc! political justice, 
fraternity, unity and national integrity." 
"It is, therefore, a mandatory duty of every political party, body of individuals 
or association and its members to abide by the Constitution and the laws". 
"A political party, therefore, should not ignore the fundamental features of the 
Constitution and the laws . . . Equally it/they should not sabotage the same 
basic features of the Constitution either influencing the electoral process or 
working of the Constitution or the law .... The political party or the political 
executive securing the governance of the State by securing majority in the 
legislature through the battle of baltot throughout its tenure by its actions and 
programmes is required to abide by the Constitution and the laws in letter and 
spirit". 
"A political party that seeks to secure power through a religious policy or 
caste orientation policy disintegrates the people on grounds of religion and 
caste. It divides the people and disrupts the social structure on grounds of 
religion and caste which is obnoxious and anthema to the constitutional culture 
and basic features." 
Mr. Justice Jeevan Reddy in his speech held as follows : -
"Given the above posltlon, it is clear that if any party or organisation seeks 
to fight the elections on the basis of a plank which has the proximate effect 
of eroding the secular philosophy of the Constitution it would certainly be 
guilty of following an unconstitutional course of action. Political parties are 
fonned and exist to capture or share State power. That is their aim. They 
may be associations of individuals but one cannot ignore the functional 
relevance. An association of individuals may be devoted to propagation of 
religion : it would be a religious body. Another may be devoted to promotion 
of culture; it would be a cultural organisation. They are not aimed at 
acquiring State power, whereas a political party does. That is one of its main 
objectives. This is what we mean by saying 'functional relevance'. One cannot 
conceive of a democratic form of Government without the political parties. 
They are part of the political system and constitutional scheme. Nay, they are 
integral to the governance of a democratic society. If the Constitution requires 
the State to be secular in thought and action. the same requirement attaches to 
14 

political parties as well. The Constitution does not recognise, it does not 
permit, mixing religion and State power. Both must be kept apart. That is the 
constitutional injunction. None can say otherwise so long as this Constitution 
governs this country. Introducing religion into politics is to introduce an 
impermissible element into body politic and an imbalance in our constitutional 
system. If a political party espousing a particular religion comes to power, 
that religion tends to become, in practice, the official religion. All other 
religions come to acquire a secondary status, at any rate, a less favourable 
position. This would be plainly antithetical to Articles 14, to 16, 25 and the 
entire constitutional scheme adumbrated hereinabove. Under our Constitution, 
no party or organisation can simultaneously be a political and a religious 
party. It has to be either. Same would be the position, if a party or 
organisation acts and I or behaves by word of mouth, print or in any other 
manner to bring about the said effect, it would equally be guilty of an act of 
unconstitutionality. It would have no right to function as a political party." 
The speech of Mr. Justice K. Ramaswamy and earlier judgements of the 
Supreme Court clearly show that activities of a political party promoting hatred or 
disharmony based on religion or caste have been placed at par. Mr. Justice 
Ramaswamy in fact quoted with approval that following paragraph from an earlier 
judgement of the court in Z. B. Bukhari Vs. Brijmohan ... 
"Our Constitution-makers certainly intended to set up a Secular Democratic 
Republic the binding spirit of which is summed up by the objectives set forth 
in the Preamble to the Constitution. No democratic, political and social order, 
in which the condition of freedom and their progressive expansion for all 
make some regulation of all activities imperative, could endure without an 
agreement on the basic essentials which could unite and hold citizens together 
despite all the difference of religion, race, caste, community, culture, creed 
and language. Our political history made it particularly necessary that these 
differences, ~hich can generate powerful emotions, depriving propel of their 
powers of rational thought and action, should not be permitted to be exploited 
lest the imperative conditions for the preservation of democratic freedoms are 
disturbed." 
By the aforesaid judgement, the Supreme Court has broken a new 
constitutional ground raising a question of far reaching importan~e ... namely, whether 
any Act of Parliament or any Rules framed thereunder can confer or continue to 
confer upon a body or association of persons the statutory status of a political party 
when its activities violate the Constitution of India, its basic features, its directive 
principles, the fundamental duties enshrined therein. Clause (e) of Article 51 A 
enjoins upon every citizen of India the duty "to promote harmony and the spirit of 
15 

common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic 
and regional or sectional diversities, to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity 
of women". 
Clause (c) of the proposed section 29 B of the bill and the suggestions 
contained in the Report of the Committee meet this very question. 
I may, however, add that deregistration of a political pany has to be 
prospective and cannot be retrospective. If during the process of any election a 
political party has indulged in activities contemplated by clause (c) and is 
subsequently deregistered, the havoc which it might have played during the process 
of election will remain undone. It therefore needs to be considered whether clause 
(3A) of Section 123 which defines corrupt practice as the promotion etc. of enmity 
or hatred between different classes of the citizens of India on ground of religion, 
race, caste, community, or language, by the candidate, or his agent or any other 
person acting with his consent should be amended to include the political pany to 
which be belongs. 
MADAN BHATIA, M.P.
