REPORT
Introduction
Seven Union Territories are enumerated in the First Schedule to the Constitution. The
Committee took up for study  and report administration of three of these viz. Andaman and
Nicobar Islands, Pondicherry and Chandigarh. The Committee undertook study visits of these
UTs. Under Articles 239 to 241 of the Constitution, administration of every union territory shall
be administered by the President through an Administrator to be appointed by him with such
designation as he may specify. The three UTs studied by the Committee are quite different from
one another. Andaman and Nicobar Islands is a territory quite far away from the mainland
comprising numerous small islands scattered in Bay of Bengal. Its southern-most point is nearer
to Indonesia. It is about 1200 km from the mainland. The UT of Pondicherry though a coastal
territory, has a Legislative Assembly. Chandigarh, a recently developed UT is the capital of two
States — Haryana and Punjab. Therefore each of these is unique in geographical locations and
administrative structures.
Chapter-I
ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR ISLANDS
Brief historical, geographical and demographic profile
2.0 The name Andaman was presumed to be derived from Hanuman, who was known to the
Malays as Handuman. Since Pre-historic times, these islands were the home of aboriginal tribes.
The tribes living in Andaman group of islands are of Negrito origin, viz. the Great Andamanese,
Onges, Jarawas, and Sentinalese, while the tribes living in Nicobars are of Mongoloid stock, viz.
the Nicobarese and Shomphens. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands were shrouded in mystery for
centuries because of their inaccessibility. The first settlement by the British in the islands took place
in 1789, which was later abandoned in 1796, The second settlement was basically a penal
settlement, taken up in 1858. During the British period political leaders, considered dangerous to
the interests of the Raj and other dreaded criminals were deported from the mainland to the Cellular
Jail-the Indian Bastille, at Port Blair. Thus these islands were infamously known as the ‘Black Water
Prison’ or ‘Kala Pani’.
2.1 The Andaman and Nicobar Islands were declared as a scheduled district in 1874 under the
Scheduled Districts Act with the main objective to provide simple and good administration in these
areas as these were inhabited by simple tribal people. Under the Government of India Act, 1919
too, the territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, being too small to have a legislature, continued
to remain under Central Legislature with powers vested in the then Governor-General to make
regulations under the Act and to extend laws of other parts of India to it as scheduled district.
The position continued under the Government of India Act, 1935 except that Governor General was
empowered to make regulations for peace and progress and for good governance of Andaman and
Nicobar Islands, Until Andaman .and Nicobar Islands came under the occupation of Japanese forces
during the Second World War, the Archipelago was used by the British Government in India as a
penal settlement, Even. after Independence the Union Constitution Committee in its Report
Submitted on October 21, 1947 favoured direct administration of Andaman and Nicobar Islands by
the Centre.

2
2.2 The Andaman and Nicobar are a group of 572 islands, islets and rocks lying in the South
Eastern Part of the Bay of Bengal with a total geographical area of 8.249 sq km with 38 inhabited
islands. They lie along an and in long and narrow broken chain, approximately North-South, over
a distance of nearly 800 kms. The Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar has been divided into
2 districts viz District of Andaman and District of Nicobars. The district of Andaman is Northern
Part of Andaman and Nicobar islands and comprises of 550 Islands, Islets and rocks out of which
only 26 are inhabited. The total provisional population of the UT according to 2001 census is
3,56,265; the decadal growth of population between 1971-81 being 63.93%. Between 1981-1991
it was 48.70% and declined to 26.94% between 1991-2001. The population density of the islands
is 43 people per sq. km. The rise in population can mainly be attributed to immigration. Within the
total population., the tribal population is about 30,000 in 2001 as compared to 26,770 in 1991
census.
2.3 In these Islands, people of all faiths-Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs etc, and speaking
languages like Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Punjabi, Nicobari etc, live together in complete peace
and harmony. Inter-religion and inter-regional marriages are Common in the Islands. Because of this
amazing racial and cultural mix, it is correctly described as Mini-India.
ADMINISTRATIVE SET UP
Panchayati Raj Instituions
3.1 The Pradesh Council in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands was constituted in June, 1981
under the provisions of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Administration) Regulation, 1979. The
Pradesh Council was an advisory body and was set up to discuss and make recommendations to
the Administrator on policy matters, plan and budget of the Union Territory and legislative matters.
It consisted of the Administrator; Member of Lok Sabha representing the Union Territory; Chairman
of the Port Blair Municipal Board and others.
3.2. W ith the establishment of the Panchayati Raj Institutions in A&N Islands, the institution of
Pradesh Council was discontinued. While Pradesh Council was an advisory body, panchayats enjoy
executive functions. The Ministry have also stated that there is no proposal to revive the Pradesh
Council.
3.3 Consequent upon the Constitution seventy third and seventy fourth Amendments, a three-
tier Panchayat System for the UT was introduced through the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
(Panchayats) Regulation, 1994 and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Municipal) Regulation, 1994.
The Andaman and Nicobar (Administration) Regulation, 1974 which provided for constitution of a
Pradesh Council was repealed on 23 May, 1994 by the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Municipal)
Regulation, 1994.
3.4 On promulgation of the A&N Islands (Panchayat) Regulation, 1994, by the President of
India, the three-tier Panchayat System was introduced consisting of 67 gram panchayats, seven
panchayat samities and one zila parishad which started functioning from October, 1995.
3.5 The elections for all the three tiers of PRIs are conducted by the Election Commission as
per provisions of A&N Islands (Panchayats/Preparation of Electoral Rolls and Conduct of Election),
Rule, 1995, notified on 28 March, 1995, for 67 gram panchayats, seven panchayat samities and
one zila parishad.
3.6 After the promulgation of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Panchayats) Regulation, 1994,
various rules have been framed for effective implementation of the provision contained in the
Regulation.

3
3.7 Under A&N Islands (panchayats) Regulation, 1994, powers have been delegated to PRIs for
implementing schemes of economic development and social justice. The regulation endows the PRIs
with powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as institutions of Self-
Government. The Regulation further authorises the panchayats to levy, collect and appropriate such
taxes, duties, tolls and fees as are specified.
3.8 The A&N Administration, vide Notification Nos.178, 179 and 180 all dated 22.12.1995 have
specified the activities to be implemented by the three tiers of PRIs. Accordingly, the Administration
has issued direction for transfer of activities of the following departments to the PRIs:
(1) Agriculture;
(2) PWD;
(3) Electricity;
(4) Fisheries; and
(5) Rural Development
3.9 The Committee was informed that, in actual practice, only the activities of PWD, i.e., rural
roads and rural water supply have been transferred to PRIs till date on a mutual agreement between
the PRIs and PWD. Even though, the activities of PWD had been transferred, funds and
functionaries required for proper upkeep and maintenance of the transferred assets were yet to be
provided. The transferred roads (182 kms) are in very bad shape and require huge amount for its
repair and maintenance.
3.10 In respect of other Departments, vis-a-vis , Agriculture, Electricity, Fisheries and Rural
Development, though the Administration had specified the functions to be transferred to the PRIs,
nothing concrete had been done so far to execute the orders of the Administration in its true letter
and spirit.
3.11 The Administration had also initiated action for transfer of activities in the field of
education, small-scale industries, farm forestry, social welfare, public distribution, health and
sanitation but orders in this regard were yet to be issued by the Administration.
Need for a Legislative Assembly
3.12 The Ministry of Home Affairs, in the written reply, stated that the matter relating to
provision of a Legislative Assembly and a Council of Ministers for the A&N Islands was considered
by the Cabinet in its meeting held on 1 October, 1997 and it decided to defer the matter.
3.13 Elaborating about the Cabinet Note of 1997, the Committee was informed that the Ministry
of Home Affairs suggested the following options in the Cabinet Note:
(a) The existing administrative set-up of the Union Territory of the Andaman and Nicobar
Islands as per provisions contained in Article 239 of the Constitution be continued;
(b) A Legislature with a Council of Ministers may be granted to the Union Territory of
the Andaman and Nicobar Islands without altering its Union Territory status, on the
pattern of administrative set-up provided to Pondicherry under the Government of
Union Territories Act, 1963.
3.14 The Cabinet, in its meeting held on 1 October, 1997, considered the proposal and decided
to defer the matter.
3.15 The Chief Secretary, Andaman and Nicobar (Administration), during the course of oral
submissions before the Committee, stated that the issue of providing Legislative Assembly had been

4
raised many times. He also felt that as per the people’s aspirations, there should be an Assembly.
He also stated that the issue of size and form of the Assembly could be decided later.
3.16 The Committee is of the view that as A&N Islands, which is headed by a Lieutenant
Governor, has no public representative to supervise, to consider or to monitor the functions
of the Government apart from the Lieutenant Governor, it can at least have a Pradesh
Council. It is also of the view that Panchayati Raj cannot be a substitute for the Pradesh
Council. PRIs will look after the execution of policies and programmes under Part IX
(Article 243 G) of the Constitution, whereas the Pradesh Council would review and
supervise the functioning of the Government.
3.17 The Committee is also given to understand that there are problems of increasing
unemployment and urbanization, law and order, bootlegging. The Committee feels that these
are directly connected with development. When the State is administered by officers only,
there is no scope for monitoring and overseeing the working of the Administration and
ultimately development is affected. When development is not taking place, people suffer
leading to increase in crime rate. These issues can be solved only by people’s participation
in governance through their elected representatives.
3.18 The Committee, during its visit to Andaman and Nicobar Islands, noted the
immensity of tsunami devastation and the problem of shortage of staff. Had there been a
Legislative Assembly the relief operation would have been addressed in a better manner.
The Committee is, therefore, of the firm view that there is a strong justification for setting
up of a Legislative Assembly for the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. It therefore,
recommends to the Government to take necessary steps in this direction.
3.19 Until a final decision is taken for setting up a Legislative Assembly, some kind of
monitoring mechanism is required. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Pradesh
Council may be revived immediately. This is all the more necessary because the
administration of the entire UT of Andaman and Nicobar Islands cannot be left to the
Panchayat Raj Institutions. These are only local self governing institutions and they cannot
be a substitute for a legislative set up.
3.20 The Committee also takes note of the fact that consequent upon the seventy third
and seventy fourth Amendments to the Constitution, though the participation of the people
in planning and execution of developmental works in the UT started at the grass-root level,
the process of delegation of powers and functions to PRls have been very slow. The subjects
apportioned to them are limited and even in those areas the transfer has not been
complete. The Committee, therefore, recommends that local bodies may be delegated more
powers and functions without further delay so that they can meet the people’s aspirations.
Further the Committee recommends that these bodies should be supported by adequate
staff, finance and other logistics.
Sociological Set up
4.0 The aboriginal tribes of the Islands have a population of approximately thirty thousand and
some of them appear to be on the verge of extinction. The anthropological reports say that the
population of one of the primitive tribes viz. Onge has come down to around hundred. This has
caused concern for the sociologists as to how the tribes can be saved from extinction and how
they can be brought into mainstream. The policy of the Government, as informed to the
Committee, in relation to the six aboriginal tribes of Andaman and Nicobar islands, has been to
protect their interests; save them from extinction; encourage them to maintain their culture and
identity; and thereby facilitate them to co-exist with the mainstream society. The Government have

5
promulgated a Regulation called “the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Protection of Aboriginal Tribes)
Regulation, 1956 so as to ensure protection of the interests of the various tribes in the Andaman
and Nicobar Islands.
4.1 Replying to a query as to whether the Government has any plan to bring the. aboriginal
tribes into the mainstream, the Ministry have informed that in the Union Territory of Andaman and
Nicobar Islands, there are five primitive Tribes, viz., Great Anadamanese, Onges, Jarawas,
Shompens and Sentinelese. Of these, presently Great Andamanese and Onges are in contact with
the outside world and in fact a few Great Andamanese are employed under the Administration.
Similar is the case with the Onges. So far as Jarawas are concerned, the Ministry of Home Affairs
in consultation with the U.T. Administration recently has formulated the Jarawa Policy in pursuance
of an order of the High Court of Calcutta in PIL No.WP048 of 1999 — Ms. Shyamali Ganguly,
Advocate vs. Union of India and Others. As per the policy no attempts to bring the  Jarawas to
the mainstream society against their conscious will or to rehabilitate them to separate islands/
locations at this stage of their social development, would be made. The Jarawa Policy has been
accepted by the Calcutta High Court. It was also stated that the Administration was following
similar policy in respect of the Shompens and Sentinelese for the time being.
4.2 When asked to comment on the future plan for the tribals of Andaman and Nicobar Islands,
particularly the primitive tribals, the Chief Secretary, Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Administration)
stated that they should not be integrated immediately into the mainstream; otherwise they will just
vanish because they will contact various diseases. This has happened with Onges and Andamanese.
He has further stated that integration is a very slow process and if they are brought directly into
the civilised world from the primitive, they would probably have a lot of problem. He has further
informed the Committee that the Ministry have a High-Powered Committee of Scientists,
Anthropologists and others who advise them on a day-to-day basis.
4.3 The Committee takes note of the fact that there are five primitive tribes in the
whole of Andaman and Nicobar Islands. They fulfil the essential characteristics of tribals.
The Committee understands the compulsion of the Government in integrating the tribal
communities into the mainstream of the society. This is a sociological process, which needs
to be addressed through the process of time only. However, the Committee notes that the
tribes are living amidst reserved forest land. These tribals, may at some point of time in
future come out and mix up with the civilised society. Therefore, some provision has to be
made so that when they enter the civilised world, they should be given an opportunity to
use the forest land and do the farming. While preserving the uniqueness of the tribals, the
process of integration into the mainstream of the society may continue as per requirement
at a particular point of time.
Administrative Issues
5.0 During the visit of the Committee to the Islands, it was informed that for better
administration., the Andaman District needs to be bifurcated and corresponding sub-division and
tehsils are also required to be created. In reply to a query as to whether the Ministry has received
any proposal from the UT Administration regarding creation of new district and sub-divisions, the
Ministry stated that the A&N Administration submitted a proposal for creation of a new District,
namely, North and Middle Andaman by dividing the existing Andaman district. The proposed new
district would have its HQs at Mayabunder. The proposal, besides creation of a new District
involves creation of corresponding Sub-Divisions and Tehsils in the new set up. It was also
informed that the proposal was under consideration of the Ministry of Home Affairs.
5.1 The Committee feels that the proposal of the Island Administration for creation of
new district and sub-divisions would help in delegation and decentralization of powers
necessary for quick decision-making. The Committee recommends that the demand of the

6
Administration may be examined on priority. The new District and sub-divisions would help
the local administration in catering the needs of people, in an efficient manner and in the
quickest possible time.
Need for helicopters
5.2 The UT Administration has taken one helicopter from M/s Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd. on
lease which has been in service from 17 May, 2003 . Another Pawan Hans helicopter was inducted
after the Tsunami disaster which was away for major repairs since 24th May, 2005.  These
helicopters are of Dauphin type which can carry 7 passengers apart from the pilot. The
Administration has informed that the helicopter has not come back as yet, despite several
reminders. However, for far-flung areas beyond Car Nicobar, the passenger capacity is reduced to
5 on account of fuel constraints.
5.3 The Committee was also informed that the helicopters ply to Campbell Bay twice a week
and Hut Bay once a week. On the other two days, (Sunday being reserved for maintenance) the
helicopter operates upto Car Nicobar. However, depending upon the needs, helicopter schedule is
varied. Post-tsunami, it is not normally operated in the northern islands since relief and
rehabilitation is essentially focusing on the southern islands.
5.4 Replying to a query as to whether the Government has any plan to augment the number
of helicopters for 572 Islands spreading over 800  kms, the Ministry informed that the Andaman
and Nicobar Administration have submitted a proposal for acquisition of two Dornier and two
Dhruv Helicopters from M/s Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. at an estimated cost of Rs.141 crore. The
A&N Administration have informed that the Planning Commission has earmarked Rs.50 crore for
this purpose during the financial year 2005-06 . The proposal submitted by the A&N Administration
is presently under consideration in the Ministry of Civil Aviation.
5.5 The Committee understands the gigantic task of the administration of 572 islands
spread over 800 kms. They need sufficient vehicles for transportation and aerial route is
the only available means for ‘inter-island transportation. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the proposal for acquisition of two helicopters may be approved at the
earliest. This will help the administration in providing necessary help to the people besides
making the helicopters available for inter-island transport on a regular basis.
Personnel Administration
5.6 The Chief Secretary informed the Committee that there was a shortage of around 3000
Group ‘C’ & ‘D’ staff in the Administration which was causing difficulty in the relief and
rehabilitation work and other ongoing projects. He felt that the long process of recruitment i.e. the
vacancies being forwarded to Ministry of Home Affairs and from there to Union Public Service
Commission for recruitment, takes a long time resulting in the vacancies remaining unfilled for a
very long time. The Chief Secretary felt that some arrangements should be made by the
Government of India to fill up the vacancies at least at lower level faster. The Special Secretary
in the Ministry, apprised the Committee that the 10% blanket ban on recruitment by the Central
Government was also applicable to the UT and a clause in that order regarding abolition of the
vacancies, which remain unfilled for two years, was a bottleneck in filling up the vacant posts,
He also apprised that out of these 3000 vacant posts, 400 posts have been sanctioned by Ministry
of Finance and other 650 are in the process of being sanctioned.
5.7 The Committee notes the difficulty being faced by the Administration due to shortage
of staff in providing relief and rehabilitation and completion of other ongoing projects. Such
a large number of vacancies for such a small administrative set-up is a matter of concern

7
particularly when relief and rehabilitation work is to be done on war footing. The
Committee recommends that the Finance Ministry’s blanket ban on recruitment for the UT
should be reconsidered. The Government should also look into the issue of delay in filling
up of vacancies and take steps to expedite the same.
Tourism in the Islands
6.0 Considering the natural and virgin beauty of the islands, tourism has been identified as one
of the thrust sectors for the economic development and employment generation in the islands. The
development of tourism can change the economic scenario in the islands and bring about significant
change in the economic well being of the local population.
6.1 In regard to opening more islands for tourism, the Ministry stated that the Island
Development Authority (IDA) in its tenth meeting held on 19.1.2003 under the Chairmanship of the
then Prime Minister decided, inter alia, to assign to a Standing Committee of Secretaries (SCOS),
a time bound responsibility of developing and recommending a policy for development of tourism,
fisheries, high-value agriculture and hydro-carbon energy sources in A&N Islands. Consequently,
the Ministry of Tourism formulated an Action Plan for development of tourism in A&N Islands. The
Action Plan proposed development of tourism in the A&N Islands in three phases. In the first
phase, it was proposed to develop tourism in the following ten islands in the Andaman and Nicobar
Islands and also opening up for foreign investment and tourism: (i) Havelock Island; (ii) Neil Island;
(iii) Long Island; (iv) North Passage Island (Merk Bay); (v) South Andaman Island; (vi) Cinque
Island; (vii) Rose and Smith Island; (viii) Little Andaman Island; (ix) Rutland Island; and
(x) Interview Island.
6.2 The Committee was also informed that the development of other islands for promotion of
tourism would be taken up in the second and third phase. The Ministry of Tourism prepared a note
for obtaining the approval of the Cabinet to the proposed action plan for development of tourism
in A&N Islands. The Ministry of Home Affairs further stated that they conveyed clearance to the
proposal contained in the draft Cabinet Note circulated by the Ministry of Tourism. The Committee
was also informed that all the above-mentioned islands would be thrown open for tourism in A&N
Islands as and when the Cabinet approves the action plan.
6.3 The objectives set in the Tenth Five-year Plan for the promotion of tourism are:
➢ Eco-friendly and environmentally sustainable tourism;
➢ Essentially playing the role of a facilitator and encouraging private sector investment
in various sectors like development of high quality resorts, introduction of high speed
boats, adventure water sports, etc.;
➢ Continuing to simultaneously concentrate on development of new tourism activities/
products; and
➢ Marketing A&N Islands as eco-tourism destination.
For achieving the above-mentioned objectives, the following schemes have been taken up:
➢ Strengthening of Directorate of Tourism;
➢ Creation, Maintenance of tourism infrastructure;
➢ Tourism promotional activities; and
➢ Strengthening and maintenance of tourist accommodation.
6.4 The Committee was informed that with the implementation of the creation and maintenance
of tourism infrastructure scheme, the direct and indirect employment generation would be about

8
5,000 persons and by implementing the strengthening and maintenance of tourist accommodation
scheme, the employment generation would be about 5,000 persons.
6.5 The Committee desires that the objectives set in the Tenth Five-Year Plan such as
ecofriendly and environmentally sustainable tourism, development of new tourism activities/
products and marketing the Islands as eco-tourism destination, etc. should be achieved. The
schemes taken up needed to be implemented on a priority basis for achieving the objectives
as this would generate employment besides strengthening tourism. The Committee also
recommends that 2006-2007 being the terminal year of the Tenth Five-Year Plan, all-out
efforts may be made so that no activity taken up remains incomplete.
6.6 On 26 December, 2004, a massive earthquake, measuring 9.3 on the Richter Scale, had hit
the Islands followed by tsunami waves which unleashed havoc and devastation causing huge
damage to life and property in the Islands. Tourism, which is the lifeline of t he Islands’ economy,
has been adversely affected by the disaster. In the post-tsunami, tourist arrivals have dipped to
rock-bottom levels. The tourist arrival in January 2004 were 13,309 which had dipped to 1335
in January, 2005. Similarly the number dipped to 1313 in February 2005 from 12011 in
February, 2004. The Committee was informed that a strategy for post-tsunami tourism development
has been prepared with short-term and medium-term objectives.
6.7 The Committee desires that the Government should address both the short-term and
medium-term objectives and take necessary steps for taking up and completion of all the
proposals in a definite timeframe.
6.8 Andaman and Nicobar Islands are the ultimate unexplored destination of India’s
tourism. Once they are open to tourists there is no doubt that the islands would become
one of the tourism attractions in the world. Despite having very good tourism potential,
India has not tapped it well. A&N Islands are a good example of this. There are many
countries in the world which thrive on tourism and India is not able to make use of the
potential. The Committee is however happy to note that things are moving in the right
direction with the opening up of more islands in A&N Islands. By opening up islands, more
investment will flow in and tourism will develop which ultimately leads to economic growth
of the islands and the country. The Committee desires that the proposal of opening more
islands for tourism may be got cleared from the Cabinet at the earliest.
Air connectivity
7. The need for an international airport at Port Blair has increased, to a great extent, with the
growing demand for air-traffic and A&N Islands being considered as tourist destination in World
Tour Map. The  main work of extension of the airstrip has been carried out with additional length
of 5000 ft, by APWD. Need for Helicopter service which will tremendously boost tourism activities
in these Islands including international tourists was also felt. This will certainly open up new vistas
of self-employment opportunities to Island youths and private entrepreneurs.
7.1 Port Blair lies on the route from the Indian mainland to South-East Asia. The A&N Islands
has vast potential for being promoted as a high-value-Iow-volume tourism destination. For this it
is important that International flights make a stopover at Port Blair, the gateway to the Islands, thus
opening the islands to international tourism. It was stated that a request for declaring of Vir
Savarkar Airport as an International Airport was made to the Ministry of Civil Aviation by the A&N
Administration way back in July, 2001. In addition, a suggestion was also made by the UT
administration to the Ministry of Civil Aviation to consider stopover of one or two flights of the
Indian Airlines on the Chennai-Singapore and Chennai-Bangkok sectors in Port Blair. But the
extended runway of the Port Blair airport is yet to be functional for operation of long haul wide-

9
bodied aircraft. This issue is being pursued by the Lt. Governor, A&N Islands from time to time
with the Minister for Civil Aviation.
7.2 The Committee was also informed that the following proposals of air connectivity have been
made as medium-term objectives as a strategy for post-tsunami tourism promotion:
➢ Introduction of direct flights from Delhi, Mumbai, Cochin and other important
destinations of the country to Port Blair;
➢ Introduction of flights by various airlines to Port Blair like Sahara, Deccan,
Kingfisher, etc., and also private chartered flights;
➢ Introduction of competitive and attractive air fares by various airlines like Apex, Super
Apex, Metro Apex, etc.;
➢ Introduction of International Airline flights for Port Blair;
➢ Introduction of International Chartered Flights for Port Blair;
➢ Declaring Port Blair as International Airport;
➢ Transfer of the operations of the airport to the Airports Authority of India;
➢ Opening of additional civilian airports in Andaman as well as Nicobar District for
landing of national and international flights as well as for operation of helicopter
services and small planes for inter-island transportation;
➢ Introduction and promotion of sea planes for national and international transportation;
and
➢ Introduction of helicopter services, small planes and sea planes by Government as well
as the private sector for inter-island transportation of tourists.
7.3 The vast potential of international tourists can only be tapped if there is world class
airport and other infrastructure. Air connectivity and tourism are inter-linked and inter-
dependent. A&N Islands, being remotely and strategically located, need better air
connectivity both domestic and international for better tourist arrivals. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry should take steps to declare Vir Savarkar Airport as an
International Airport as a step towards projecting A&N Islands as an attractive tourist
destination. The Committee also recommends that to begin with the Government can make
the stopover for Chennai-Bangkok and Chennai-Singapore flights at the Islands. It also
urges upon the Administration to complete the expansion work of the airport expeditiously,
thus making it capable for operation of wide-bodied aircraft. The Committee is also of the
view that the other proposals in the strategy for post-tsunami tourism promotion, if
implemented, will go a long way in the promotion and strengthening of tourism in Andaman
and Nicobar, Islands, particularly the proposal relating to introduction of flights from
various cities to Port Blair will go a long way in attracting tourists from different
destinations of the country to the Islands. The Committee desires that the above proposals
may be taken up on top priority.
AGRICULTURE AND FISHERY
8.1 The years between 1927 to 1931 were actually the beginning of Agriculture Department in
the Islands with main task of experimenting in coconut plantation, coffee garden and 16 village
demonstration plots, when agriculture was negligible. The area expansion for increasing production
was the main theme up to the end of Fourth Five-Year Plan, i.e., 1974. From the Fifth Plan,

10
intensive agriculture was the practice due to paucity of land, and by the Seventh Plan, various.
developmental activities through different schemes began. During this post-Independence
development era, a lot of commercial crops were introduced which are now successfully growing
in these Islands.
8.2 In Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the total available land for agriculture is limited to 50,000
ha., i.e., six per cent of the total geographical area only. The Ministry have stated that no further
land was being released because of the prevailing ecological conditions. Due to rapid urbanisation
and growth of population in these Islands, arable land is shrinking while pressure on enhancing
productivity is enormous. It was also stated that strategy was adopted to keep a balance among
the various uses of land to increase production and productivity in a sustainable manner and efforts
were being made to produce more per unit area by adopting multiple and intensive cropping system
following the scientific management practices with utmost care of conserving soil and water.
Further, efforts are underway to utilise the vacant hilly land by promoting plantation, fruits and
spices crops, which grow naturally well out here.
8.3 On a query as to whether there was any proposal to diversify farming and fishing in the
Islands by promoting shrimp/crab culture, it was stated that the Ministry of Agriculture and
Cooperation (Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying), the administrative Ministry, had
indicated that since freshwater resources were very limited in ‘the Union Territory of Andaman and
Nicobar Islands, there was not much scope for freshwater aquaculture. However, suitable areas
could be identified and earmarked for undertaking coastal shrimp culture in the Union Territory.
The Central Institute of Brackishwater Aquaculture (CIBA) in collaboration with the Central
Agricultural Research Institute (CARl) working under the Department of Agriculture Research and
Education (DARE) may take up identification of suitable areas for coastal shrimp culture. It was
also stated that the UT Administration may allot suitable lands to shrimp farmers on a long-term
lease.
8.4 The Committee is of the view that considering the vast potential of fisheries, shrimp,
crab and prawn, concerted efforts need be made to explore the potential by diversifying
fishing to Shrimp, Crab and Prawn culture. The issue of identification of suitable areas for
coastal shrimp culture may be pursued with Central Institute of Brackishwater Aquaculture
(CIBA). This is necessary in view of scarcity of freshwater in the Islands. The Committee
notes that land available in the Islands is very less and its optimum use should be made.
Besides diversifying farming practices, efforts should also be made to increase productivity.
Efforts being made to utilise vacant hilly land for plantation, spices, crops, etc., may be
intensified as these are eco-friendly and they grow naturally. Similarly, diversification of
agriculture by encouraging plantation of cash crops such as cashew nuts, spices, and coconut
in the Islands might prove to be a panacea for improving the economic condition of the
farmers and the tribals living in the region.

CHAPTER-II
PONDICHERRY
BRIEF HISTORICAL, GEOGRAPHICAL AND DEMOGRAPHIC PROFILE
9.1 The Territory of Pondicherry was merged with the Indian union with effect from
01.11.1954 in accordance with the agreement between the Government of India and
the Government of France. However, the de-jure transfer of Pondicherry took place on
16 August, 1962 and since then the Union Territory of Pondicherry has been administered under
the provisions of Government of Union Territories Act, 1963. The Union Territory of Pondicherry
consists of four regions namely Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam which are lying
geographically separated from one another. Pondicherry region which is on the east coast, about
162 kms. south of Chennai is the largest of these areas. The Union Territory of Pondicherry is
480 sq. kms. in area and has a population of 9,74,345 according to the 2001 census. The male
and female population, respectively, is 4,86,961 and 4,87,384, registering a sex ratio of 1,001
females for every 1000 males. The Scheduled Castes population is 1,57,771 and accounts for
16.19% of the total population.
STATEHOOD TO PONDICHERRY
9.2 The UT of Pondicherry has an elected Legislative Assembly and a Council of Ministers.
During the visit to Pondicherry, the Committee interacted with the Chief Minister and his ministerial
colleagues besides holding a meeting with the MLAs. There was an unanimous feeling among the
elected people’s representatives that power was concentrated in the Executive, i.e., the Lieutenant
Governor and in turn the Union Home Ministry. The people’s representatives were of the view that
the political aspirations of the people could be fulfilled only by granting full statehood to the UT.
The Committee was apprised that the Legislative Assembly, Pondicherry, had passed Resolutions
from 1971 to 2004 for grant of statehood to Pondicherry and sent the same to Government of
India for consideration. The Resolutions passed on 9.6.2000, 26.6.2001 and 30.7.2004 sought
granting of statehood with special category status to the Union Territory.
9.3 The Special Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs, during the course of his oral
submissions before the Committee stated that according to the criteria of the Planning Commission,
special category status was given to States on the basis of the criteria which include strategic
location on the border with neighbouring countries, hilly terrain, inadequate economic and social
infrastructure, predominantly large tribal population and limited and weak revenue base compared
to the development needs. Planning Commission had taken the view that Pondicherry did not
have such disadvantages and, therefore, it had ruled out granting Special Category status to
Pondicherry.
9.4 Replying to a query regarding the status of the proposal of statehood of Pondicherry
Government, the Ministry in its written response informed that the proposal submitted by the
Government of Pondicherry for granting statehood with special category status vide its
Memorandum dated September 2004 was not accepted by the Government of India on the
following grounds:—
(a) It is not eligible to be considered for a special category status as per the guidelines
of the Planning Commission.
11

12
(b) It is not a viable State economically . Out of its total budget of about Rs.1050 crores
in the year 2004-05, there was a revenue deficit of over Rs. 400 crores.
(c) It consists of four geographi cally, culturally and l inguistically separate segments. While
Pondicherry and Karaikal are Tamil speaking, Mahe is Malayalam speaking and Yanam
is Telugu speaking.
(d) The per capita income of Pondicherry is almost double to that of neighbouring Tamil
Nadu. Therefore, it cannot be said that development has suffered for want of
Statehood.
9.5 The Chief Secretary, Pondicherry, during the course of his oral submissions before the
Committee, stated that according to 11th Finance Commission, if at all Pondicherry was to become
a State, it should be given a Special Category status. According to the Chief Secretary, most of
the powers have now been delegated to the Chief Minister as well as Lieutenant-Governor. Both
of them are having administrative as also financial powers. He further stated that in other States,
files stop at the level of the Chief Minister whereas in Pondicherry, all the important files would
go upto the Lieutenant-Governor.
9.6 The Special Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, when asked by the Committee to clarify
about the next step to be taken by the Government in the matter, stated that according to the
Government, it was not correct to give the Special Category status now and some more time was
necessary.
9.7 The Committee takes note of the views expressed by a section of the society in
Pondicherry and feels that the sentiments of the people and the people’s elected
representatives cannot be ignored. The overwhelming view of all of them is in favour of
Statehood to the Union Territory of Pondicherry with Special Category status. The
Committee feels that the aspirations of the people have to be respected. The Committee
takes due note of the views of the Ministry that it will not be a viable State economically.
But the Committee cannot be oblivious to the fact that when Goa graduated into a State,
there were apprehensions that Goa might not sustain as a State because of its weak
financial base. But, today, Goa has proved it otherwise. Further, Pondicherry has a
Legislative Assembly with elected representatives.
9.8 The Committee is also given to understand that Pondicherry Government appointed
a Committee to go into its viability as a State and the then Chief Secretary of Pondicherry
had submitted the Report; the Report was examined and it was agreed, in principle, by the
Government that it would bring forward a Bill in the Parliament to grant Special Category
Status to Pondicherry. However, this proposal was shelved.
9.9 Looking at the practical point of view, the Committee is of the view that Pondicherry,
as a Union Territory, is a big handicap for the Chief Minister to function. Most of the
administrative powers are vested in the Lieutenant-Governor and files are cleared by him.
9.10. T aking into account all these factors, the Committee is of the view that the issue of
Statehood to Pondicherry needs to be considered in a holistic manner. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Government may consider granting Statehood to Pondicherry with Special
Category Status.
B-II CATEGORY STATUS TO PONDICHERRY
10.1 The issue of upgrading Pondicheny to B-II category from ‘C’ category for the purpose of
HRA was raised at different levels during the visit of the Committee. It was contended that whereas

13
Port Blair and Panaji having less than 2 lakh population had been accorded the status of B-1 category,
Pondicherry was being deprived of the same. The Ministry while responding to the issue has
informed that the matter was referred to Ministry of Finance and that the Ministry of Finance has
stated that the proposal for grant of B-II category to Pondicherry had been considered in detail earlier
also but could not be agreed to because cities/towns were classified/reclassified on the basis of their
population as reflected in the decennial census report. Moreover, for the purpose of grant of HRA,
the population within the municipal area of the city is taken into account. As per census of 2001,
the population of Pondicherry (UA) was 5,05,959 and that of Pondicherry (MC) 2,20,865.
Accordingly, Pondicherry (UA) is classified as ‘B-ll’ for the purpose of CCA and ‘C’ class for HRA.
The Ministry also stated that since it does not fulfil the existing criteria i.e. the population of
Municipal limit area should be between 5-10 lakh for Classification of a city into B-II class as
recommended by the 5th Central Pay Commission and accepted by the Government. Therefore, the
demand for upgradation of Pondicherry as B-II class city for grant of HRA could not be agreed to.
10.2 The Special Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, during the course of his oral submissions
before the Committee, mentioned that the Pondicherry Government had recommended for its
upgradation but it could not be acceded to as the Ministry of Finance was not agreeable to the
same.
10.3 The city of Pondicherry, which is also the capital of the UT of Pondicherry has been
undergoing a rapid transformation. It has all the characteristics of a developed urban
agglomeration. The Committee takes note of the fact that the population of urban
agglomeration of Pondicherry exceeded 5.05 lakhs as per the Census of 2001. The rapid
growth of administration, industrialization, educational institutions; the population of urban
agglomeration exceeding five lakhs; the floating population of about one lakh per day, justify
the grant of B II status to Pondicherry. The Committee is also given to understand that Port
Blair and Panji were granted B II status, even though their population was less than that of
Pondicherry. The Committee expresses its concern over the discriminatory attitude shown
towards Pondicherry. When Port Blair and Panaji have been granted B II status, the
Committee cannot buy the argument given by the Government in respect of Pondicherry.
B II status, besides increasing HRA to Government employees will also enhance the status
of the city. The city will be able to get urban development schemes and more opportunities
for development. The Committee therefore strongly recommends that Government may grant
B II status to Pondicherry city for the purpose of payment of HRA. The Committee urges
upon the Government that “the relaxation made in the case of the cities of Port Blair and
Goa in this regard may also be extended to Pondicherry so that the officials of the Central/
UT Government are adequately compensated for their expenditure on housing.
RECOGNITION OF SCHEDULED TRIBES IN PONDICHERRY
11.1 During its visit to Pondicherry, the Committee came to know that people belonging to
Scheduled Tribes do not enjoy the status of Scheduled Tribes and the facilities accompanying it
such as reservation in education, employment, etc. in Pondicherry. This was causing problem for
the ST communities as their brethren in neighbouring districts of Tamil Nadu were getting the
benefit of reservation facility whereas they were being deprived of the same. Replying to a query
as to the reason for  excluding the STs from the demographic profile of the UT and that whether
the Government had any plan to provide reservation to the STs in Pondicherry, the Ministry of
Home Affairs forwarded the following facts given by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs:
“Constitution of India does not define Scheduled Tribes as such. Article 366 (25) refers to
Scheduled Tribes as those tribes or tribal communities who are scheduled in accordance
with Article 342 of the constitution. This Article states that only those communities who

14
have been declared as such by the President through an initial public notification will be
considered as Scheduled Tribes. Any further amendment in the list is through an Act of
Parliament. The list of Scheduled Tribes is State-specific and a community declared as
Scheduled Tribe in a State need not be so in another State. No community has been
specified as Scheduled Tribes in relation to the States of Haryana and Punjab and Union
Territories of Chandigarh, Delhi and Pondicherry. It further stated that the essential
characteristics were first laid down by the Lokur Committee. It mentioned that for  a
community to be identified as Scheduled Tribe the following characteristics were
required:—
(i) Indication of Primitive traits;
(ii) D istinctive culture;
(iii) Shyness of contact with the public at large;
(iv) Geographical isolation; and Backwardness-social and economic.
As per the modalities fixed for deciding inclusion in, exclusion from  and other modification
in the list of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes approved in June, 1999, if the
concerned State Government recommends the proposal and forwards it to the Central
Government, it is sent to the Registrar General of India (RGI). The RGI, if satisfied with
the recommendations of the State Government, recommends the proposal to the Central
Government. Thereafter, Central Government refers the proposal to the National
Commission for Scheduled Tribes (erstwhile National Commission for SCs and STs) for
their recommendation. After the National Commission recommends, the matter is processed
for the decision of the Cabinet. According to the above procedure, only those cases that
have been agreed to by the concerned State Government, Registrar General of India as well
as National Commission for STs, are considered for amending legislation. After the decision
of the Cabinet, a Bill is introduced in Parliament. In case, a proposal is not supported by
the RGI, it is referred back to the State Government for reviewing or further justifying their
recommendations in the light of the observations of the RGI and these proposals remain
under consideration till an agreement is reached between the concerned State Government
and the RGI as to fulfilment of the criteria by the community concerned.”
11.2.1 The Ministry of Home Affairs further stated that the UT Administration of Pondicherry had
recommended for inclusion of various communities in the list of Scheduled Tribes since 1982
onwards. The Registrar General of India in his report dated 18.8.1992 had, inter-alia reported that
the communities which were trying to seek their notification as Scheduled Tribe in relation to
Pondicherry represent a migrant stock with no cultural roots in the UT and did not answer the
laid down criteria. The proposal was referred to the UT Admn. for reviewing or further justifying
their recommendations in the light of the observations made by the RGI. The UT Administration
of Pondicherry vide their letter dated 2.09.2003 recommended five communities for inclusion in the
Scheduled Tribes list. Their details are given below:—
(i) lrular (including Sub-tribes of Irular);
a. Villi
b. Vettaikaran
(ii) Mlaikuravan;
(iii) Kattunayakan;
(iv) Yerukula; and
(v) Kuruman

15
UT Administration of Pondicherry requested the Ministry of Home Affairs to include the
above communities in the list of STs on the basis of recommendations made in the “Report
of identification of the Scheduled Tribes of Pondicherry-An ethnographic Study” prepared by
Dr. T. Subramanyam Naidu, Head of Department of Anthropology and Centre for Future Studies,
Pondicherry University, Pondicherry. The recommendation of the UT was again sent to RGI for
their comments on 16-0-2004. However, the UT Administration was requested on 5.7.2004 to send
a comprehensive ethnic study of each tribe to justify their inclusion with supporting information
to the Ministry. The UT Administration had forwarded a copy of the report prepared by
Dr. T. Subramanyam Naidu, Head of Department of Anthropology and Centre for Future Studies,
Pondicherry University, Pondicherry, to the Ministry on 20.7.2004 which was handed over to the
Office of the RGI. The RGI vide their D.O. No. 8/1/04-SS (Pondicherry) dated 7-2/2005 was of
the view that the claims of the above communities for inclusion in the list of ST of UT of
Pondicherry were not justified. The Committee was further informed that the comments of the RGI
had been referred to the Government of Pondicherry for further justification on the claims of above
communities, vide this Ministry’s letter dated 2.5.2005.
11.2.2 The Committee expresses its concern that even though the UT Administration of
Pondicherry has been recommending for recognition of the Scheduled Tribes, the Registrar
General of India has not taken any positive decision so far. His views on five criteria are
not pragmatic and hence may be dispensed with. The Committee also notes that the above
mentioned tribes existed in UT of Pondicherry even before its independence in 1954, as per
the reports of Backward Classes Commission of Pondicherry. The Committee is of the view
that RGI is procrastinating the matter. Keeping in view the existence of scheduled Tribes
as identified by the Government of Pondicherry, Backward classes commission and the
Ethnographic study of Dr. Subramaniyam Naidu, the Committee recommends notification by
Government of the five Scheduled Tribes identified by the UT Administration of Pondicherry
in terms of Articles 342 read with Article 366 (25) of the Constitution.
ELECTION TO PANCHA YATI RAJ INSTITUTIONS
12.1 Panchayats, evolved in ancient India, are one of the oldest democratic systems still in use
today. They have been the backbone of the Indian villages since the beginning of recorded history.
Gandhiji, the father of the nation, had aptly remarked that Indian Independence must begin at the
bottom and every village ought to be a republic or Panchayat having powers. Mahatma Gandhi
advocated Panchayati Raj, as the foundation of India’s political system. The Constitution (Seventy-
Third Amendment) Act, 1992 provides for establishment of a three-tier structure (Village Panchayat,
Panchayat Samiti or Intermediate-level Panchayat and Zila Parishad or District-level Panchayat);
establishment of Gram Sabhas at the village level and regular elections to Panchayats every five years.
12.2 The Constitution (Seventy- Third Amendment) Act, 1992 also envisages empowered
Panchayats as institutions of self-government at the village level capable of:
➢ Planning and executing village level public works and their maintenance; and
➢ Ensuring welfare of the people at the village level including health, education,
communal harmony, social justice, particularly gender and caste-based discrimination,
dispute resolution, welfare of children, especially the girl child.
12.2.1 A rticle 243 E (3) provides as under:
“An election to constitute a Panchayat shall be ccmpleted-
(a) before the expiry of its duration specified in clause (1);
(b) before the expiration of a period of six months from the date of its dissolution;

16
Provided that where the reminder of the period for which the dissolved Panchayat would
have continued is less than six months, it shall not be necessary to hold any election under
this clause for constituting the Panchayat for such period.”
12.3 The Committee during its visit to Pondicherry, was informed that elections to Panchayat Raj
Institutions (PRIs) have not taken place in the UT for the last thirty years. Replying to a query,
the Secretary, Panchayati Raj informed the Committee that Court’s stay was the reason for not
holding PRI elections in the UT, and that it had been vacated and Administration was ready to hold
election any time.
12.4 The Committee expresses its deep concern over the fact that in spite of the
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) having been granted constitutional status, and under
Articles 243 (K) and (L) of the Constitution regular elections are required to be held to the
panchayats every five years, elections thereto have not been held in Pondicherry for the
last 30 years. In this connection, the Committee takes notes of the constitutional provision
under Article 243 E (3). The Committee takes strong exception to the non-compliance of the
constitutional obligation. The Committee is happy to learn that the order for conducting
elections to Panchayati Raj Institutions has been issued recently.
PERSPECTIVE PLAN FOR TOURISM DEVELOPMENT
13.1 Pondicherry has a rich French Cultural heritage, having been the capital of the French
Colonies in India since the 17th  Century. Pondicherry region, with a coastal line of 45 Kms, well

the ideal place for spending holidays with family. The tourism potential of Pondicherry is not fully
tapped. In view of providing adequate and better facilities to visiting tourists the administration with
the help of the Government of India has been jointly taking efforts to boost tourism activities.

Ministry of Home Affairs have stated that in the field of Tourism UT Government has following
perspective plan:—
– “Operationalization of Pondicherry Airport and extension of the existing runway in
order to operate ATR/Boeing type aircrafts.

The train will cover the southern States such as Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Karnataka,

To provide an enabling environment of attracting private investment in the tourism
sector (for the construction of hotels, resorts, entertainment parks etc.) the
Government of Pondicherry is offering the following subsidies:—

13.3 The Committee feels that in view of the historical significance and geographical
location, Pondicherry has the potential to develop into a good tourist destination. The
Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Pondicherry Government in making
it as an ideal tourist destination. Airports are an important ingredient for growth of tourism
and in that direction the Committee recognizes the necessity of Pondicherry and Karaikal
airports. The Committee recommends that the Central Government should make all efforts
for early operationalisation of the Pondicherry Airport and establishing of Karaikal Airport.
The Committee also recommends that the development of Pondicherry and Karaikal Ports
and Art and Craft Village in Murungapakkam may be taken up and completed at the
earliest as these would give good infrastrucutral support required for tourism. Construction
of Star Hotels may also be taken up and the development of Medical Tourism may be

AGRICULTURE AND IRRIGATION
14.1 Alth ough agricultural growth in Pondicherry had been negative in the nineties, it has made
considerable progress on a number of fronts. Improved crop production technologies have been
adopted, crop and irrigation intensities have increased and a network of support institutions and
infrastructure have been developed. However, agricultural productivity has remained low and not
increased perceptibly during the last ten years. In addition, there are emerging signs of land
degradation, poor soil management and excessive exploitation of water resources.
14.2 The Ministry of Home Affairs stated that it had become necessary for the Government of
UT of Pondicherry to reorient agriculture production so as to enable the farmers to produce for
the market. This required transfer of knowledge and skills to them. Hence the department decided
to open Uzhavar Udhaviyagams (Farmers’ Help Centres) for  each revenue village which would
ultimately be the knowledge hub of the villages. It would be a one-stop solution for the various
problems being faced by the farming community. Towards this end, the Government of UT of
Pondicherry proposes to introduce large scale diversification of agriculture, encourage less water
intensive and more profitable horticulture production, mechanization, introduction of concepts of
hi-tech and precision agriculture, close co-ordination and interaction between the Government
Agriculture College (PAJANCOA) and the farming community, introduction of post-harvest
technologies like setting up of cold storage plants, rural godowns etc., setting up of market
forecasting centers, introduce contract farming in floriculture activities like orchids, wide spread
use of computers and internet etc., are the thrust areas of the current year.

18
14.3 The Committee expresses its concern over the fast declining net area sown and low
agricultural productivity in the last ten years. Productivity remaining static, land
degradation, poor soil management and excessive exploitation of water resources indicate
the poor health of agriculture sector. The proposal of the UT of Pondicherry to open Uzhavar
Udhaviyagams (Farmers’ Help Centres) is a path-breaking solution to the ills ailing the
farm sector. The Committee is happy to learn that the plan has been implemented and feels
that it should be pursued in the right perspective.
FISHERY DEVELOPMENT
15.1 The Union Territory of Pondicherry comprises of four maritime regions with 45 Kms of a
coastal line and 675 sq. kms of inshore waters. Various development oriented plans and welfare
schemes are implemented with an objective to augment marine, inland and brackish water fishery
production and to develop socio-economic conditions of fishermen community. The Ministry of
Home Affairs informed that the UT of Pondicherry proposed to increase the fish production to
57,000 MT by the end of Tenth Plan.
15.2 T sunami left a major impact on the fishermen community in UT of Pondicherry. 599 people
died in Pondicherry due to the killer tidal waves of tsunami, out of which 492 in Karaikal and 107
in Pondicherry. The fishermen had borne the brunt of tsunami and the losses incurred by them are
heavy, both in terms of lives lost and damage to the fishing rafts.
15.3 When the Committee sought to know about the Government’s plans to rebuild the affected
region for diversifying agriculture and fishery by promoting crab/shrismp culture, etc. the Ministry
of Home Affairs stated as under:
“A comprehensive plan for modernizing the fishing activities being planned as a part of
World Bank assisted project to increase the fish production of this territory and also to
substantially enhance the living standard of fishermen in this territory. It includes
reconstruction of fishing village, modernization of fishing vessels, introduction of fishing
trawlers, training of fishermen on modem fishing technology etc. Regarding promotion of
Shrimp culture, clearance of aquaculture, authority of India is needed for any renewal and
formation of new farms. Action is being taken to identify the uncultivable lands suitable for
shrimp culture. It is also stated that the 12 Shrimp farms with an extent of 36.28 Ha. Of
area at Karaikal has been affected by recent tsunami disaster on 26.12.2004.”
15.4 The Committee is of the view that early action is needed to bring the people
belonging to agricultural and fishermen communities affected by Tsunami, back to
normalcy. Some rehabilitation measures have already been taken. Now, it is time that
sufficient infrastructure is in place so that they could start leading normal life. The
Committee desires that the comprehensive plan for modernizing fishing activities initiated
by the Government may be implemented at the earliest. For promotion of shrimp culture
clearance of Aquaculture Authority may be obtained at the earliest. Identification of
cultivable land may be completed soon so that shrimp culture may be developed at the
earliest.

CHAPTER-III
TSUNAMI-REHABILITATION AND RECONSTRUCTION
Andaman and Nicobar Islands
16. The massive earthquake and resultant tsunami, which occurred on 26.12.2004, caused
unprecedented damage to life and property. Extensive damage was reported from Car Nicobar,
Katchal, Chowra, Nancowry, Great Nicobar, etc., in the Nicobar District and Netaji Nagar and Hut
Bay in Andaman District. The earthquake and Tsunami caused extensive damage in Port Blair
harbour, jetties at Aberdeen, Phoenix Bay, Junglighat and Haddo were flooded by tidal waters. In
the Islands, 3513 persons are reported to have lost their lives (including those missing and
presumed dead).
16.1 The disaster left a severe impact on livelihood. Fishermen living on the coasts lost their
boats and fishing nets. The disaster caused an enormous environmental impact which will affect
the region for many years to come. It has been reported that severe damage has been inflicted on
ecosystems such as mangroves, coral reefs, forests, coastal wetlands, vegetation, rock formations,
animal and plant biodiversity and groundwater. The main effect is being caused by poisoning of
the freshwater supplies and the soil by saltwater infiltration and deposit of a salt layer over arable
land. Wells that served communities were invaded by sea, sand and earth; and aquifers were
invaded through porous rock. The saline soil becomes sterile, and it is difficult and costly to
restore the same for agriculture. It may also cause the death of plants and important soil
micro-orgarnisms.
16.2 The Committee, during its visit to Andaman and Nicobar Islands, made a study of the
impact of tsunami tidal waves on Andaman and Nicobar Islands and held discussions with a cross-
section of the people. The Member of Parliament representing the Union Territory stated that the
effect of tsunami was enormous and about 10,000 houses were to be constructed but the various
restrictions regarding forest conservation were an impediment in the rehabilitation work for
construction of permanent houses. He pleaded for payment of cash instead of built-up houses for
them. Further, he stated that Government should provide interest free loans for development of
trade and commerce which was totally ruined. Augmentation of helicopter service in view of
the strategic position of the Islands was also sought by him. He was of the view that
timely disbursement of compensation was very vital for building people’s confidence in the
Government.
16.3 The representatives of Tsunami affected people were of the view that interest free housing
loan should be provided to them. Every affected family should be provided with at least one
Government job. Compensation should be granted to the next of kin of those who had died as was
given to the victims of avalanche disaster in J&K.
16.4 The Committee. also visited the Tsunami affected villages (Tamaloo and Chuk Chuka) of
Car Nicobar to see the intermediate shelters and interacted with the people and their representatives
called Captains, Vice-Captains. They expressed reservations about the permanent shelters proposed.
to be built of concrete and steel. They wanted construction of permanent shelters with local
materials which could be expanded later on for accommodating more members of their families.
Since iron is prone to rust due to salinity it was told to be unfit for rehabilitation units.

20
17. Explaining about the damage to the agricultural land due to tsunami, the Development
Commissioner stated that the total area damaged was 10837 hectares out of which paddy and other
field crops were on 1730 hectares whereas plantation crops were on 9107 hectares. The total area
under submergence was 4339 hectares comprising paddy and other field crops. The total
reclaimable area was 6561 hectares which consisted of 694 hectares of paddy and other field crops
and 5867 hectares of plantation crops. He mentioned that a total number of 6020 farmers were
affected out of which 1743 were in Andaman district and 4277 in Nicobar district. The total
financial loss was to the tune of Rs. 321 crore. The Commissioner mentioned that out of a total
livestock/poultry of 10,85,739 in the Islands before Tsunami, 1,57,577 livestock/poultry were lost
due to tsunami for which Rs. 11.83 crore as compensation was sanctioned by Government of
India.
Rehabilitation and Reconstruction
18. Explaining about the rehabilitation efforts made, the Ministry of Home Affairs, in their
written note, stated that the Rajiv Gandhi Relief Package, announced immediately after the Tsunami,
had an outlay of Rs. 821.88 crore. Out of the outlay of Rs. 821.88 crore for immediate relief and
rehabilitation, an amount of Rs. 532 crore was sanctioned during the financial year 2005-06, out
of which an amount of Rs. 519.81 crore had been spent. Rs. 235 crore has been sanctioned for
the current year. The Ministry of Home Affairs also stated that construction of 9565 shelters was
organised for temporarily housing homeless families and these have been fully occupied. The
construction of these shelters was done in a record time of about two-and-a-half months, well
before the onset of monsoon last year.
18.1 The Government has recently approved (December, 2005) a long-term reconstruction
programme for restoring the infrastructure and livelihood in Andaman and Nicobar Islands with a
total outlay of Rs. 2677.91 crore. It is to be implemented over a period of three years. As part
of the reconstruction programme, the Government of India has approved a programme for
construction of 9714 permanent houses for the victims. The whole programme would be
implemented under the overall supervision of Ministry of Urban Development. Excavation work has
started in 20 out of 25 clusters. Construction materials have started reaching the Islands. The
target date for completion of the shelters is December, 2007, except for the shelters at Campbell
Bay which are dependent on construction of roads that are planned.
18.2 Relief for small traders and businessmen: The Ministry have also stated that revival
package for small traders and businessmen in Andaman and Nicobar Islands has been approved
under which outstanding amount in respect of loans up to Rs. 2 lakh as on 26.12.2004 will be
written off from the books of financial institutions. For loans beyond Rs. 2 lakh and up to
Rs. 5 lakh, normal interest on outstanding principal amount as on 26.12.2004 will be waived off
for three years. The total value of this package is Rs. 57.51 crore. A proposal for further
enhancing this package is under consideration.
18.3 Compensation for loss of crop:  The compensation for loss of crops was substantially
enhanced by the Government of India. As against the original rate of Rs. 4,000/- per hectare for
plantation crops, the rate has been enhanced to Rs. 90.465/- per hectare. In the case of other
agricultural crops, the rate has been enhanced from Rs. 1,000/- to Rs. 2,500/-. per hectare to
Rs. 22,231/- per hectare. The enhanced package is under implementation.
18.4 Special Package for Agriculture:  A special agricultural package of Rs. 239.54 crore under
Rajiv Gandhi Relief Package for reclaiming agricultural land that was damaged has been approved
for Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Such a package has not been approved for any other State.
Under this programme, the following activities have been undertaken:

21
➢ Repair and reconstruction of dykes;
➢ Cleaning of debris of affected areas;
➢ Application of organic manure in plantation crops area;
➢ Rainwater harvesting through construction of check dams; and
➢ Supply of pumpsets.
19. The tsunami tidal waves have caused widespread devastation in the Islands resulting
in loss of human life as well as livestock besides loss of property. The Committee feels that
considering the magnitude of destruction of life and property, whatever rehabilitation that
has been provided would not match the loss caused by the natural calamity. But the relief
provided will mitigate the suffering though the scares may not be removed permanently.
However, the Government should not leave any stone unturned to ensure early
rehabilitation of the affected people and to undertake reconstruction process to ensure that
they start their normal life at the earliest. The Committee understands that the
Government have taken up several relief measures. In regard to construction of permanent
houses, the Committee feels that the permanent shelters should be at locations which are
high on ground near the earlier habitations as the livelihood of the people requires them
to continue residing there. Similarly, while constructing the houses, use of local material
such as bamboo, wood, etc., should be preferred as they are earthquake-resistant and give
better protection from sun. The Committee also takes note of the fact that some people,
who met the Committee during its visit, desired that money may be provided to their
families so that they can construct their houses themselves. This is a better proposition
because it will engage the families in the reconstruction work till the completion of the
construction. The Government may, therefore, consider providing them financial help
besides other required material to enable the families engage themselves in the
reconstruction work.
19.1 The Committee has noted that revival package for small traders consists of waiver
of loans and interest thereon, etc. The Committee recommends that the Government may
consider increasing the package of Rs. 57.15 crore further. It also recommends that the
Government may consider providing interest-free fresh loans for at least two years to
enable them to start their business afresh. Though the Government has given compensation
for loss of agricultural crops which is now Rs. 22,231 per hectare, this is a pittance
considering the fact that agricultural land has now become saline and uncultivable and
barren. It can no longer be used for any agricultural activities and even grass will not grow.
Therefore, the Government should consider providing some package for permanent
rehabilitation of the farmers whose agricultural land is no longer useful. The package may
also contain providing assistance for business or employment.
19.2 The Committee feels that the request of the people in the islands for employment
to at least one person in each affected family needs to be considered. A one-time creation
of employment opportunities would give permanent relief to the families. Besides this,
filling up of 3000 vacant posts would also cover a large number of people. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Government may consider these proposals immediately and
take decisions thereon.
Pondicherry
20. The killer tidal waves of tsunami triggered by series of earthquakes of unprecedented scale
off the Indonesian Coast struck the coastal areas of the Union Territory of Pondicherry on the early

22
hours on 26 December, 2004. The tsunami waves hit the coasts of South India with such ferocity
and suddenness that it has turned out to be the deadliest natural disaster in the recent history,
bringing huge devastation of catastrophic proportions. Coastal fishing community and some of the
poorest people living in the coastal regions were the most affected with huge loss of lives as well
as fishing crafts and tackles and destruction of habitat and houses. Children and women were
affected most adversely as they were the least able to resist and were dragged into watery graves.
An estimated 30,000 people became homeless in the Union Territory of Pondicherry. The death toll
was 599 - 492 in Karaikal and 107 in Pondicherry.
20.1 Sixteen villages in Pondicherry and seventeen villages in Karaikal have been affected. 17,432
people in Karaikal and 26,000 people in Pondicherry have been displaced. The agricultural crop in
792 hectares of land has been damaged. Owing to the tsunami 10,061 houses were damaged.
Twenty-two relief camps were set up in Karaikal and twenty-six in Pondicherry to take care of
the relief operations of about 30,000 victims of tsunami during its peak period of functioning.
20.2 El aborating upon the relief operations, the District Commissioner, Karaikal stated that 15000
people were brought to the twenty-two relief camps within ten days of Tsunami tragedy. They
were provided with rice, kerosene and other cooking materials. NGOs also helped by way of
community kitchen. The Government also provided relief to fishermen who lost their boats
depending upon the fishing craft. The compensation of Rs. 3750/-  per hectare, as immediate relief,
was given for sea water intrusion in the agricultural fields. Another Rs 60000/-per hectare would
be given to them to take steps to restore the productivity of land. For loss of cattle also
compensation was provided on a certain yardstick. He mentioned that 1200 temporary shelters were
constructed and Rs 1000/- per family was provided for repair of houses. For constructing
permanent shelters land had been identified and required modalities were being worked out.
20.3 Reflecting upon relief and rehabilitation measures, the Relief and Rehabilitation
Commissioner stated that there were twenty-two relief centers at Karaikal and twenty-six at
Pondicherry. Ex gratia payment of Rs. 1 lakh each was made to the families of the deceased and
an amount ranging from Rs. 5000 to Rs. 4.5 lakh were given for various items such as funeral
expense, medical expense, housing subsidy for damaged houses, purchase of catamarans/boats,
wooden mechanized boats, etc. Besides this, Rs. 3750/- was also immediately given to each farmer
for damage to crops.
20.4 Rajiv Gandhi Relief Package:  The Ministry of Home Affairs have stated that immediately
after tsunami hit the coastal area of Pondicherry on 26 December, 2004, the Government of India
sanctioned an amount of Rs. 155.62 crore under the Rajiv Gandhi Rehabilitation package to the
Pondicherry Government for the purpose of immediate relief and rehabilitation measures.
20.5 Tsunami Rehabilitation Programme:  The Government has recently approved in
December, 2005, a long-term reconstruction programme for restoring the infrastructure and
livelihood in Pondicherry. This long-term reconstruction programme has a total outlay of
Rs. 518.08 crore.
20.6 Housing Reconstruction: It was further stated the Government of Pondicherry has planned
to construct 10,061 permanent houses for the victims. These will be spread over 34 settlements.
The Government of Pondicherry has formulated a Government Order governing the involvement of
the NGOs with a novel idea of insisting the NGOs to deposit 10 per cent to 20 per cent of the
project cost in any nationalised bank in the name of the NGO themselves but governed by a
tripartite agreement restricting the withdrawal of the amount by the concerned NGO after
completing 85 per cent of the work. So far, 15 MoUs have been signed with NGOs for
construction of 5,042 houses in 23 settlements. The total project cost amounts to Rs. 42.45 crore.
A total extent of 57-62-74 hectares has been acquired to facilitate construction of houses by the

23
NGOs. Out of 10,061 houses, 341 houses have already been completed and 4,827 houses are under
various stages of construction. Land acquisition is in progress for construction of remaining 4,893
houses.
20.7 Emergency Tsunami Reconstruction Project Under World Bank Aided Project:  The
Ministry have also stated that a World Bank aided project with an outlay of Rs. 158 crore for
providing permanent shelter and restoration of livelihood programme is under implementation. The
Pondicherry Government has constituted a Society namely Project Implementation Agency (PIA)
under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 to serve as an umbrella agency to implement the
assistance given by the World Bank and to undertake various other activities related thereto for
relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction in various sectors. So far the agency has taken up
construction work at 3 villages and development of infrastructural facilities in 8 villages. This apart,
the agency has taken up the work of filling up of low-lying areas where the NGOs have been
assigned with construction of houses for the affected persons.
21. The Committee notes that about 800 hectares of agricultural land as well as crops
were affected by the tidal waves in Pondicherry. Much of the land may remain permanently
unfit for farming. The relief given may not give permanent compensation to the affected
people. In all the cases of permanent loss of land, the Committee suggests that the
Government may consider raising the compensation appropriately.
21.1 After Tsunami, many farmers have been severely affected with many children getting
orphaned. Though Government has provided relief package and rehabilitation, it may also
consider providing permanent compensation in the form of reservation in employment to
such victims. This is all the more necessary in the case of orphaned children.
21.2 In regard to construction of permanent houses, the Committee expresses its concern
that out of 10, 061 houses, only 341 houses have been completed so far and it feels that
this way it is going to take a long time for completing all the houses. The Committee
recommends that the pace of construction may be increased and all the houses may be
completed within a definite time frame. Land acquisition for construction of houses may be
completed at the earliest so that construction may start at the earliest.
21.3 The World Bank aided project is an appreciable effort of the international agency.
Government may monitor the project so that targets are achieved within the given time
frame.
