Additional DG, SSB responded that by and large the officers in the force are happy after being
combatised. Elaborating upon it, he said that except few, officers want to get combatised because
they gain in terms of various allowances.
4. Members raised issues such as para whether any consideration/weightage is given to people
residing in border areas in recruitment in BGFs who being familiar with the topography are better
acclimatized and more suited for such forces, whether there are any guidelines for specifying the
area from border on which funds earmarked for development of border areas are to be utilized,
the problems being faced by farmer residing in areas where fencing has been done on International
Border on account of regulated entry/exit to their fields falling on other side of the fencing,
difficulties faced by SSB in effective guarding of some areas on Indo-Nepal border in Bihar due
to intermittent floods in the riverine areas, non availability of mobile phone services in such areas
due to prohibition of installing mobile phone towers upto 10-12 kms from border, illegal migration
of Maoists into India from Nepal through the said border, etc.
5. The Home Secretary and the Additional DG , SSB responded to the queries of the Members
and assured the Committee that the pother matters would be examined in the Ministry.
6. The Committee then took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill as under:
Clause 2
6.1 Clause 2 seeks to define the various expressions used in the Bill. Sub-clause 1 (a) of this
clause defines ‘active duty’ broadly speaking according to this definition, a member of the Force
will be on active duty during the period he is attached to, or forms part of, a unit of the Force:—
(i) Which is engaged in operations against an enemy, or (ii) Which is operating at a picket or

24
engaged on patrol or other guard duty along the borders of India. And includes duty by such
person during any period declared by the Central Government by Order as a period of active duty
with reference to any area in which any person or class of persons subject to this Act may be
serving. Certain offences such as under clauses 18, 22 and 23 are punishable more severely when
committed on active duty. The definition is modeled on the definition of ‘active duty’ in the Indo
Tibetan Border Police Force Act, 1992.
6.1.1 Sub-clause 1 (i) of the Clause defines enemy and reads “Enemy includes all armed
mutineers, armed rebels, armed rioters, pirates and any person in areas against whom it is the duty
of any person subject to this Act to take Action”. A member observed that this definition of
‘enemy’ is lacking as it does not contain words “to prevent trans-border crimes and unauthorized
entry or exit from the territory of India”, although illegal migration and smuggling are the major
concerns on Indo-Nepal Border.
6.1.2 On the issue of deficient definition of enemy in clause 2 of the Bill, the Home Secretary
accepted the observation that the definition of enemy is deficient and needs to be reconsidered,
however he felt that including illegal migrants in the definition would not be appropriate as it
involve some involve some humanitarian aspects and some international covenants to which India
is a signatory.
6.1.3 The Committee recommended suitable amendment in the clause to make the definition of
enemy more relevant.
6.1.3 Subject to above, the Committee adopts the clause.
Clause 3
6.2 Clause 3 seeks to specify the persons subject to the proposed legislation.
6.2.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 4
6.3 Clause 4 seeks to provide for the constitution of the Sashastra Seema Bal.
6.3.1 The Committee recommended that the Government should reconsider Clause 4 so as to
expand the role of SSB to include the duty of spreading security awareness and security
consciousness among the people of border areas. The Committee feels that in the present
atmosphere the SSB will not be able to do justice with its initial role after its full combatisation.
Hence it recommends that although its combatised wing should be strengthened for border guarding
role, which has been assigned to it on the basis of recommendations of the Group of Ministers
on Reforming National Security System, its non-combatised wing should not be phased out as has
been proposed because in its absence the SSB will not be able to do the great service it was doing
as its stay behind role during external aggression and its peacetime role.
6.3.3 Subject to above, the Committee adopted the clause.
Clause 5
6.4 Clause 5 seeks to provide for the general superintendence, direction and control of the
Force and appointment of officers of the Force.
6.4.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 6
6.5 Clause 6 seeks to deal with enrolment of persons to the Force.

25
6.5.1 Members expressed serious concerns on the provision of the Bill for enrollment of non-
citizens in the SSB. The Home Secretary clarified the reasons for incorporating the provision such
as the treaty with Nepal and Bhutan for employment of their people in India and others, however
agreed to reconsider the provision either on the lines of what is their in the ITBP Act, 1992 or
by removing it altogether from the Bill.
6.5.2 The Committee recommended that the provision in clause 6(2) of the Bill for enrolling the
non-citizens for a limited period after approval of the Central Government, having regard to the
special services required in the interest of security of the borders of India should be removed. It
also recommended that even if the services of non-citizens are to be obtained the provision should
be on the lines of ITBP Act or these services should be taken by non-citizens without enrolling
them as is being done in RAW and IB.
6.5.3 Subject to above, the Committee adopted the clause.
Clause 7
6.6 Clause 7 seeks to provide for liability of members of the Force for service in and outside
India.
6.6.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clauses 8 to 12
6.7 Clauses 8 to 12 seek to deal with tenure of service, etc. of members of the Force.
6.7.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clause 13
6.8 Clause 13 seeks to impose certain restrictions on the rights of members of the Force to
form association and on their freedom of speech etc.
6.8.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clauses 14 and 15
6.9 Clauses 14 and 15 seek to provide for remedy of aggrieved persons including officers.
6.9.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clausea 16 to 48
6.10 Clauses 16 to 48 seek to constitute offences under the proposed legislation and penalize the
members of the Force for the various acts prejudicial to the maintenance of discipline, good order
and efficiency of the Force. These clauses follow subject to certain modifications, the provisions
relating to offences contained in sections 16 to 48 of the Indo Tibetan Border Police Force Act,
1992. The modifications relate to inclusion of offences in relation to terrorists.
6.10.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clauses 49 and 50
6.11 Clauses 49 and 50 seek to lay down that all civil offences committed by the members of
the Force within or beyond India shall be deemed to be the offences under the proposed legislation
and shall be triable by a Force Court. Exception under section 50 has, however, been made in

26
respect of the civil offences of murder, culpable homicide not amounting to murder and rape in
relation to civilians where such offences are committed by the members of the Force while not
on active duty.
6.11.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clause 51
6.12 Clause 51 seeks to set out the various punishments which may be awarded by Force
Courts.
6.12.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 52
6.13 Clause 52 seeks to enable a Force Court to take into account the nature and degree of the
offence committed and award to the person convicted of any offence under clauses 16 to 48 the
punishment prescribed by the relevant provision or punishment lower in the scale within the
meaning of clause 51.
6.13.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 53
6.14 Clause 53 seeks to set out the punishments which may be awarded in combination by a
Force Court.
6.14.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 54
6.15 Clause 54 seeks to provide that enrolled person sentenced on active duty by a Force Court
to imprisonment whether combined with dismissal or not, may be retained to serve in the ranks
and such service shall be reckoned as part of his term of imprisonment.
6.15.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clauses 55 to 59
6.16 Clauses 55 to 59 seek to deal with imposition of certain minor punishments for offences
under the proposed legislation without the intervention of a Force Court. Clause 56 seeks to
authorize a commanding officer of and above the rank of Commandant to proceed in the prescribed
manner against any person other than an officer or Subordinate officer and award one or more
punishments specified therein. Clause 57 imposes certain limitations in respect of award of these
punishments. Clause 58 authorises an officer not below the rank of Inspector-General to proceed
in prescribed manner against an officer of or below the rank of Commandant and award one or
more punishment specific in the clause. Clause 59 provides for review of proceedings under clause
58 by the prescribed authority in the prescribed manner.
6.16.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clause 60
6.17 Clause 60 seeks to provide for imposition of collective fines in case of loss or theft of
weapons or ammunition of a unit upon the subordinate Officers, under-officers and men of such

27
unit considered to be responsible for the loss or theft. To avoid abuse, it has been provided that
the power can be exercised only by an officer not below the rank of commandant of a unit.
6.17.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clauses 61 to 68
6.18 Clauses 61 to 68 seek to provide for deductions that may be made from the pay and
allowances of officers and other persons subject to the proposed legislation.
6.18.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clauses 69 to 74
6.19 Clauses 69 to 74 seek to deal with arrest and proceedings before trial. Clause 69 provides
that any person charged with an offence under the proposed legislation may be taken into Force
custody under the order of a Superior Officer but an officer who is engaged in a quarrel, affray
or disorder may be ordered into Force custody by even an officer inferior in rank. Clause 70
provides for the action that has to be taken after arrest. The charge against every person taken
into Force custody must be investigated within forty-eight hours unless investigation within that
period is impracticable having regard to the public service. In case of delay the matter has to be
reported to superior authorities. Clause 71 provides that in every case where any person who is
not on active duty remains in force custody for a longer period than eight days without a Force
Court for his trial being convened, a special report giving reasons for the delay should be made
by the Commanding Officer and a similar report should be forwarded at intervals of every eight
days until a Force Court is convened or such person is released from custody. Clauses 72 and 73
provide for assistance of magistrates, police officers and other civil authorities in the matter of
apprehension and arrest of persons accused of offences under the proposed legislation and
deserters from the Force. Clause 74 provides for inquiry into absence without leave of a person
subject to the proposed legislation.
6.19.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clause 75
6.20 Clause 75 seeks to provide for appointment of Force police officers and defines their
functions and duties. The Force police officers are intended to serve as the internal police of the
Force.
6.20.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 76
6.21 Clause 76 seeks to provide for three kinds of Force Courts, namely General Force Courts,
Petty Force Courts and Summary Force Courts, for the trial of offences under the proposed
legislation.
6.21.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clauses 77 to 86
6.22 Clauses 77 to 86 seek to deal with convening of Force Courts, the composition of Force
Courts and their powers.
6.22.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.

28
Clause 87
6.23 Clause 87 seeks to provide that a person subject to the proposed legislation who has been
acquitted or convicted of an offence by a Force Court or a Criminal Court or who has been dealt
with under clause 56 or clause 58 (relating to imposition of minor punishments by certain officers)
shall not be liable to be tried again by a Force Court or dealt with under the said clauses. It thus
prohibits a second trial in respect of the same offence.
6.23.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 88
6.24 Clause 88 seeks to prescribe a three-years period of limitation for trial of all offences under
the proposed legislation except the offences of desertion and mutiny.
6.24.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 89
6.25 Clause 89 seeks to deal with the liability of a person who has ceased to be subject to the
proposed legislation after the commission of an offence thereunder.
6.25.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 90
6.26 Clause 90 seeks to provide for the continued application of the proposed legislation during
the term of sentence.
6.26.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 91
6.27 Clause 91 seeks to deals with place of trial.
6.27.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clauses 92 and 93
6.28 Clauses 92 and 93 seek to deal with choice of forum for the trial of offences in respect
of which both a Force Court and a Criminal Court have concurrent jurisdiction.
6.28.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clauses 94 to 118
6.29 Clauses 94 to 118 seek to deal with the procedure of Force Courts and are based upon
sections 94 to 120 of the Indo Tibetan Border Police Force Act, 1992. In  particular, clause 99
seeks to apply provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 to all proceedings before a Force Court.
6.29.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clauses 119 and 120
6.30 Clauses 119 and 120 seek to provide provision for tendering of pardon to accomplice.
These clauses are on the lines of the provisions, in this regard, contained in the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973.

29
6.30.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clauses 121 to 132
6.31 Clauses 121 to 132 seek to deal with confirmation and revision of findings and sentence
of Force Courts. These clauses follow closely the provisions contained in sections 121 to 132 of
Indo-Tibetan Border Police Force Act, 1992 and Sections 104 to 114 of the National Security
Guard Act, 1986.
6.31.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clauses 133 to 152
6.32 Clauses 133 to 152 seek to deal with execution of sentences of Force Court, pardon of
persons convicted by such courts, remission or suspension of such sentences, etc. These clauses
follow closely the provisions contained in section 133 to 152 of the Indo Tibetan Border Police
Force Act, 1992.
6.32.1 The Committee adopted the clauses without any change.
Clause 153
6.33 Provides for powers and duties conferrable and imposable on members of the Force. This
clause empowers the Central Government to direct exercise of such powers and discharge of such
duties by members of the Force as are exercisable or dischargeable by an officer of the
corresponding or lower rank under any Central Act. This clause also empowers the Central
Government to confer or impose, with the concurrence of a State Government, any powers or
duties under the State Act upon the members of the Force of corresponding rank.
6.33.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 154
6.34 Clause 154 seeks to provide for protection of acts of member of Force.
6.34.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 155
6.35 Clause 155 seeks to deals with the powers of the Central Government to make rules.
6.35.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 156
6.36 Clause 156 seeks to provide that the existing Sashastra Seema Bal shall be deemed to be
the Sashastra Seema Bal constituted under the proposed legislation and makes the necessary and
saving provisions in regard to persons appointed to the existing Sashastra Seema Bal and as to
actions taken and things done in relation to the constitution of the existing Sashastra Seema Bal.
6.36.1 The Committee adopted the clause without any change.
Clause 1, The Enacting Formula and the Title
6.37 Clause 1, the enacting formula and the title were adopted without any change.

4. ( 1) There shall be an armed force of the Union called
the Sashastra Seema Bal for ensuring the security of the
borders of India and performing such other duties as may be
entrusted to it by the Central Government.
(2) Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Force shall
be constituted in such manner as may be prescribed and the
conditions of service of the members of the Force shall be such
as may be prescribed.
5. ( 1) The general superintendence, direction and control
of the Force shall vest in, and be exercised by, the Central
Government and subject thereto and to the provisions of this
Act and the rules made in this behalf, the command and
supervision of the Force shall vest in an officer to be appointed
by the Central Government as the Director-General of the
Force.
(2) The Director-General shall, in the discharge of his
duties under this Act, be assisted by such member of Additional
Directors-General, Inspectors-General, Deputy Inspectors-
General, Additional Deputy Inspectors-General, Commandants
and other officers, as may be appointed by the Central
Government.
6. ( 1) The persons to be enrolled to the Force, the mode
of enrolment and the procedure for enrolment shall be such as
may be prescribed.
(2) A person other than a citizen of India shall not be
enrolled in the Force except with the approval of the Central
Government, granted for a limited period, having regard to the
special services required in the interest of the security of
borders of India.
7. Every member of the Force shall be liable to serve in any
part of India as well as outside India.

any other lesser term but excluding imprisonment for a term

(d) compulsory retirement from the service;
(e) imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months
in Force custody;

or a place in the list of their rank in the case of an under-
officer;

Additional Judge Attorney-General or of the accused before the

dissolve the same if it appears to him that the exigencies of the
service or necessities of discipline render it impossible or
inexpedient to continue the said Force Court.

94. At every General Force Court or Petty Force Court, the
senior member shall be the presiding officer.
95. (1) Every General Force Court shall, and every Petty
Force Court may be  attended by a Judge Attorney or a Deputy
Judge Attorney-General or an Additional Judge Attorney-

96. (1) At all trials by a General Force Court or by a Petty
Force Court, as soon as the Court is assembled, the names of the
presiding officer and members shall be read over to the accused,
who shall thereupon be asked whether he objects to being tried by
any officer sitting on the Court.
(2) If the accused objects to such officer, his objection and
also the reply thereto of the officer objected to shall be heard and
recorded, and the remaining officers of the Court shall, in the
absence of the challenged officer decide on the objection.
(3) If the objection is allowed by one-half or more of the
votes of the officers entitled to vote, the objection shall be allowed,
and the member objected to shall retire, and his vacancy may be
filled in the prescribed manner, by another officer subject to the
same right of the accused to object.
(4) When no objection is made, or when an objection has
been made and disallowed, or the vacancy of an officer has been
filled by another officer under sub-section ( 3) to which no objection
is made or allowed, the Court shalI proceed with the trial.

be administered to every member of the Force Court and to the
Judge Attorney, or, as the case may be, the Deputy Judge Attorney-
General or the Additional Judge Attorney-General or the officer

(2) Every person giving evidence before a Force Court shall
be examined after being duly sworn or affirmed in the prescribed
form.
(3) The provisions of sub-section ( 2) shall not apply where
the witness is a child under twelve years of age and the Force
Court is of opinion that though the witness understands the duty of
speaking the truth, he does not understand the nature of an oath or
affirmation.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
The Special Service Bureau (SSB) was raised in 1963 under the Cabinet
Secretariat in the back drop of Chinese aggression. The organitisation was
initially functional in the region of the then North East Frontier , North Assam,
North Bengal, hills of Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu.
Subsequently, its activities were extended to other border areas in Manipur,
Tripura, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Mizoram, South Bengal,
Nagaland and some areas of Kashmir valley. In January, 2001, on transfer of the
Special Service Bureau from Cabinet Secretariat to Ministry of Home Affairs, the
Special Service Bureau was assigned with the new role of border guarding force
on Indo-Nepal and Indo-Bhutan Borders. The name of Special Service Bureau
was changed to Sashastra Seema Bal with effect from 27th March, 2004.
Considering the nature and purpose of the Force and experience gained during
the last four decades, it has been felt that the Force should be regulated by a
separate self-contained statute which will provide for its special needs of
efficiency and discipline.
2. As the Sashastra Seema Bal is charged with the guarding of the Indo-
Nepal and Indo-Bhutan borders, the Bill seeks to ensure that the standards of
efficiency and discipline of the Force are of a high order.
3. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

Notes On Clauses
Clause 2  defines the various expressions used in the Bill.
Sub-clause (1)(a) of this clause defines ‘active duty’. Broadly speaking,
according to this definition, a member of the Force will be on active duty during
the period he is attached to, or forms part of, a unit of the Force—
(i) which is engaged in operations against an enemy, or
(ii) which is operating at a picket or engaged on patrol or other
guard duty along the borders of India,
and includes duty by such person during any period declared by the Central
Government by Order as a period of active duty with reference to any area in
which any person or class of persons subject to this Act may be serving;
Certain offences such as under clauses 18, 22 and 23 are punishable
more severely when committed on active duty. The definition is modelled on the
definition of ‘active duty’ in the Indo Tibetan Border Police Force Act, 1992.
Clause 3 specifies the persons subject to the proposed legislation.
Clause 4 provides for the constitution of the Sashastra Seema Bal.
Clause 5 provides for the general superintendence, direction and control
of the Force and appointment of officers of the Force.
Clause 6 deals with enrolment of persons to the Force.
Clause 7 provides that members of the Force shall be liable to serve in
and outside India.
Clauses 8 to 12 deal with tenure of service, etc., of members of the
Force.
Clause 13 seeks to impose certain restrictions on the rights of members
of the force to form association and on their freedom of speech, etc.
Clauses 14 and 15 provide for remedy of aggrieved persons including
officers.
Clauses 16 to 48 provide for offences under the legislation and the
penaltises therefor, for the various acts prejudicial to the maintenance of
discipline, good order and efficiency of the Force.
Clauses 49 and 50 seek to provide that all civil offences committed by
the members of the Force within or beyond India shall be deemed to be the
offences under the proposed legislation and shall be tribale by a Force Court.
Exception under section 50 has, however, been made in respect of the civil
offences of murder, culpable homicide not amounting to murder and rape in
relation to civilians where such offences are committed by the members of the
Force while not on active duty.

93
Clause 51 lays down the various punishments which may be awarded by
Force Courts.
Clause 52 enables a Force Court to take into account the nature and
degree of the offence committed and to award to the person convicted of any
offence under clauses 16 to 48 the punishment prescribed by the relevant
provision or alternative punishment lower in the scale under clause 51.
Clause 53 sets out the punishments which may be awarded in
combination by a Force Court.
Clause 54 provides that enrolled person sentenced on active duty by a
Force Court to imprisonment whether combined with dismissal or not, may be
retained to serve in the ranks and such service shall be reckoned as part of his
term of imprisonment.
Clause 55 to 59 deal with imposition of certain minor punishments for
offences under the proposed legislation without the intervention of a Force
Court. Clause 56 seeks to authorise a commanding officer of and above the rank
of Commandant to proceed in the prescribed manner against any person other
than an officer or subordinate officer and award one or more punishments
specified therein. Clause 57 imposes certain limitations in respect of award of
these punishments. Clause 58 authorises an officer not below the rank of
Inspector-General to proceed in the prescribed manner against an officer of or
below the rank of Commandant and award one or more punishments specified
in the clause. Clause 59 provides for review of proceedings under clause 58 by
the prescribed authority in the prescribed manner.
Clause 60 provides for imposition of collective fines in case of loss or
theft of weapons or ammunition of a unit upon the subordinate officers, under-
officers and men of such unit considered to be responsible for the loss or theft.
To avoid abuse, it has been provided that the power can be exercised only by
an officer not below the rank of Commandant of a unit.
Clauses 61 to 68 provide for deductions that may be made from the pay
and allowances of officers and other persons subject to the proposed legislation.
Clauses 69 to 74 deal with arrest and proceedings before trial. Clause 69
provides that any person charged with an offence under the proposed legislation
may be taken into Force custody under the order of a superior officer but an
officer who is engaged in a quarrel, affray or disorder may be ordered into
Force custody by even an officer inferior in rank. Clause 70 provides for the
action that has to be taken after arrest. The charge against every person taken
into Force custody must be investigated within forty-eight hours unless
investigation within that period is impracticable having regard to the public
service. In case of delay the matter has to be reported to superior authorities.
Clause 71 provides that in every case where any person who is not on active
duty remains in Force custody for a longer period than eight days without a
Force Court being convened for his trial, special report giving reasons for the
delay should be made by the commanding officer and a similar report should be
forwarded at intervals of every eight days until a Force Court is convened or
such person is released from custody. Clauses 72 and 73 provide for assistance
of magistrates, police officers and other civil authorities in the matter of
apprehension and arrest of persons accused of offences under the proposed

94
legislation and deserters from the Force. Clauses 74 provides for inquiry into
absence without leave of a person subject to the proposed legislation.
Clause 75 provides for appointment of Force police officers and defines
their functions and duties. The Force police officers are intended to serve as the
internal police of the Force.
Clause 76 provides for three kinds of Force Courts, namely General
Force Courts, Petty Force Courts and Summary Force Courts, for the trial of
offences under the legislation.
Clauses 77 to 86 deal with convening of Force Courts, the composition
of Force Courts and their powers.
Clause 87 provides that a person subject to the proposed legislation who
has been acquitted or convicted of an offence by a Force Court or a Criminal
Court or who has been dealt with under clause 56 or clause 58 (relating to
imposition of minor punishments by certain officers) shall not be liable to be
tried again by a Force Court or dealt with under the said clauses. It thus
prohibits a second trial in respect of the same offence.
Clause 88 prescribes a three-years period of limitation for trial of all
offences under the proposed legislation except the offences of desertion and
mutiny.
Clause 89 deals with the liability of a person who has ceased to be
subject to the proposed legislation after the commission of an offence
thereunder.
Clause  90 provides for the continued application of the proposed
legislation during the term of sentence.
Clause 91 deals with place of trial
Clauses 92 and 93 deal with choice of forum for the trial of offences
in respect of which both a Force Court and a Criminal Court have concurrent
jurisdiction.
Clauses 94 to 118 deal with the procedure of Force Courts. In particular,
clause 99 seeks to apply provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 to all
proceedings before a Force Court.
Clauses 119 and 120 make provision for tendering of pardon to
accomplice and trial of such persons not complying with conditions of pardon.
These clauses are on the lines of the provisions, in this regard, contained in the
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
Clauses 121 to 132 deal with confirmation and revision of findings and
sentence of Force Courts.
Clauses 133 to 152 deal with execution of sentences of Force Court,
pardon of persons convicted by such courts, remission or suspension of such
sentences, etc.
Clause 153 provides for powers and duties conferrable and imposable on
members of the Force. This clause empowers the Central Government to direct
exercise of such powers and discharge of such duties by members of the Force

95
as are exercisable or dischargeable by an officer of the corresponding or lower
rank under any Central Act. This clause also empowers the Central Government
to confer or impose, with the concurrence of a State Government, any powers
or duties under the State Act upon the members of the Force of corresponding
rank.
Clause 154 provides for protection of acts of members of Force.
Clause 155 deals with the powers of the Central Government to make
rules.
Clause 156 provides that the existing Sashastra Seema Bal shall be
deemed to be the Sashastra Seema Bal constituted under the proposed legislation
and makes the necessary and saving provisions in regard to persons appointed
to the existing Sashastra Seema Bal and as to actions taken and things done in
relation to the constitution of the existing Sashastra Seema Bal.

96
FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM
Clause 4 of the Bill provides for the constitution of the
Sashastra Seema Bal. Clause 5 provides for appointment of certain
officers of the Force. Clause 6 provides for enrolment of persons
to the Force. Clause 75(1) deals with appointment of officers of the
Force and clause 95 deals with appointment of Judge Attorney-
General and other officers of Force Court.
2. The Sashastra Seema Bal in existence at the
commencement of this Act shall be deemed to be the Force
constituted under clause 4 of the Bill.
3. All expenses incurred in connection with the administration
of this Force would be met from the Consolidated Fund of India.
As the Force is already in existence, no additional expenditure of a
non-recurring nature is likely to be involved when the Bill is enacted
and brought into force. The expenditure on the administration of the
Force during 2005-2006 was of Rs. 612.92 crores.
4. No expenditure of a non-recurring nature is involoved.
96

97
MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION
Clause 155 of the Bill empowers the Central Government to
make rules for carrying into effect the provisions of the proposed
legislation. The matters in respect of which such rules may be made
include the constitution, governance, command and discipline of the
Force, the appointment and conditions of service (including
deductions from pay and allowances) of members of the Force, the
convening, constitution, adjournment, dissolution and sitting of
Force Courts, the procedure to be followed by such Courts and
other matters relating thereto, the constitution, procedure and
practice of courts of inquiry, recruitment and conditions of service
of Judge Attorney-General and other officers of his set-up, etc.
2. The matters in respect of which rules may be made under
clause 155 are essentially matters of detail or procedure and are
merely ancillary to the proper implementation of the legislation. The
delegation of legislative power is thus of a normal character.

A
BILL
to provide for the constitution and regulation of an armed force of the Union for ensuring the
security of the borders of India and for matters connected therewith.
(Shri Shivraj Vishwanath Patil, Minister of Home Affairs)

99
ANNEXURE-II
REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY TO THE QUESTIONNAIRE
PREPARED BY THE SECRETARIAT ON THE BILL
(i) Question:–
Whether the original role of the SSB for which it was constituted still exists? if not,
reasons therefor and if yes than who is performing that role/function?
Answer:–
The role of SSB has changed from a “stay behind role” in the event of external aggression
under the Cabinet Secretariat to a ‘Border Guarding Force’ under the Ministry of Home Affairs in 2001.
Pursuant to the acceptance of the recommendations of Group of Ministers (GoM) on
Reforming National Security System administrative control of the SSB was transferred to Ministry
of Home Affairs from Cabinet Secretariat with effect from 15.1.2001. The GoM recommended the
principle of one Border, one Force for better accountability and also recommended the necessity
of comprehensive Border management including management of Indo-Nepal and Indo-Bhutan
Border. Accordingly Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has entrusted the SSB with the task of
guarding Indo-Nepal border stretching over 1751 kms in the States of Uttaranchal, Uttar Pradesh,
Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim and Indo-Bhutan border stretching over 699 kms in the States of
Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh and also designated it as the Lead Intelligence
Agency (LIA) in the areas of deployment.
(ii) Question:–
What were the experiences of the Force and what deficiencies were noticed during
the last four decades, which led Ministry to consider the proposed legislation?
Answer:–
SSB till date has no Act of its own and is currently governed under the provisions of the
CRPF Act and Rules by way of administrative arrangements. Now that the role of the Force has
been changed to a Border Guarding Force (BGF), it is administratively required to clothe it with
an independent Act of its own which is similar to the other BGFs. The proposed legislation is
intended to provide to SSB statutory backing and equip it with a separate and independent identity
at par with the other BGF’s and administrative/disciplinary structure. As SSB was not a BGF in
the past, the two situations cannot be compared.
(iii) Question:-
What is the import of the previous and the present nomenclature of the force? what
are the changes in the charter of duties of the SSB before and after its restructure? please
furnish comparative details.
Answer:–
SSB was raised on the philosophy that security of the country’s borders was not the sale
responsibility of armed forces but also required a well-motivated and trained border population,
hence was entrusted the task or promoting national integration and security consciousness among
border population. With the motto of Service, Security and Brotherhood SSB was given
99

100
nomenclature as Special Service Bureau. Under the Cabinet Secretariat SSB was a covert
organization. After having been assigned the role of a Border Guarding Force, the Special Service
Bureau was renamed as Sashastra Seema Bal w.e.f. March 27, 2004.
The normal peace time activities of the SSB are geared to the objective of getting closer
to the people in the remote border areas, win over their confidence, bring them into the mainstream
of national life and prepare them for a grave national emergency of the kind that threatened the
country in 1962.
Upon transfer of the administrative control of Special Service Bureau from the Cabinet
Secretariat to the Ministry of Home Affairs and having been assigned the role of a Border Guarding
Force, Sashastra Seema Bal is now manning the Indo-Nepal and the Indo-Bhutan Border. It is also
the Lead Intelligence Agency in the areas of deployment. The charter of duties of SSB after
restructuring is as under:–
(i) to promote a sense of security among the people living in the border areas;
(ii) to prevent trans-border crimes and unauthorized entry into or exit from the territory
of India; and
(iii) to prevent smuggling and any other illegal activities.
(iv) Question:–
What are the reasons for earmarking the force for two borders? whether the number
of the personnel in the Force is sufficient for guarding these two borders?
Answer:–
Indo-Nepal and Indo-Bhutan Borders have been unmanned by any Border Guarding Force
in the past. Keeping in view the continuity and similarity of these two borders MHA assigned the
task of guarding these Borders to SSB. The Indo-Bhutan Border also happens to be much smaller,
stretching 699 kms as compared to 1751 kms of Indo-Nepal Border. Additional manpower of 20
Bns have been sanctioned to SSB to enable it to man these two borders.
(v) Question:–
Whether any other CPMF personnel are also being deployed on these two SSB
guarded Borders? If so, how it is being co-ordinated?
Answer:–
SSB is the only CPMF deployed on Indo-Nepal and Indo-Bhutan Borders for guarding these
borders.
(vi) Question:–
Whether the services of the SSB personnel are treated as service in Field Areas? If
so, what are the criteria?
Answer:–
The SSB personnel are performing border guarding duties which is considered as service
in the field area on the same lines and pattern of personnel of BSF and ITBP.
(vii) Question:–
(a) What provisions have been made for the residential accommodation and other field
facilities for the personnel of the Force?
Answer:–

101
Consequent upon the deployment along Indo-Nepal and Indo-Bhutan Border, SSB has
undertaken the task of acquisition of land and building of infrastructure in right earnest.. In cases
where land has been taken into possession residential accommodation is being provided in the form
of pre-fabricated structure and semi-permanent structures to begin with. SSB have developed a
five-year work plan for construction of residential and non-residential buildings at all Field
formations. Regarding other field facilities for the personnel of the Force same are being provided
on the pattern of BSF, ITBP etc.
(b) Whether any field allowance has been contemplated for these personnel?
Answer
At present, no field allowance is admissible for SSB personnel. However, SSB personnel are
entitled for other allowances, as admissible to other Border Guarding Forces, at comparable locations.
Question:–
Clause 6 provides for enrolment of a non-citizen for a limited period in the Force
with the approval of the Central Government.
(a) What is the rationale for this provision particularly when there is no such provision
in other Border Guarding Forces?
(b) Whether the citizens can perform those special services which have been
contemplated for non-citizens for incorporating this provisions?
(c) What special inputs are envisaged from the non-citizens?
Answer:–
In this connection it is worthwhile to mention here that the SSB Draft Bill 2006 has been
framed on the basis of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police Force Act-l992 in which enrolment has been
defined in clause-6 which is as follows:–
“6. Enrolment—The persons to be enrolled to the Force, the mode of enrolment, and the
procedure of enrolment shall be such as may be prescribed”.
In the process of finalization of the SSB Draft Bill, 2006 a thorough examination of the
instant clause was conducted and it was observed that clause-6 of the ITBPF Act-1992 provides
a scope for enrolment of non-citizens as per policy of the Government of India in vogue which
envisages that citizens of Nepal and Bhutan can be appointed to posts in Central Government.
In view of the deployment of SSB on the Indo-Nepal and Indo-Bhutan Border it was
considered appropriate not to induct citizens of Nepal and Bhutan in SSB contemplating that such
enrolment may create problems in the effective vigil of these borders. Taking into consideration the
above said administrative aspects and that no such provision exists in BSF Act 1968 and ITBPF
Act,1992 it was felt necessary to incorporate an additional sub-clause to clause — 6 in the SSB
Draft Bill, 2006 as below:–
“(2) A person other than a citizen of India shall be enrolled in the Force except
with the approval of the Central Government, granted for a limited period, having regard
to the special services required in the interest of the security of Borders of India”.
It is worthwhile to mention that the aforesaid addition to the clause was made with an
intention to exercise an administrative check on recruitment of non-citizens, simultaneously keeping
the possibilities of such enrolment through specific permission of the Central Government for a
limited period. It is an exception and not the rule.
However, there is no objection even if the clause of recruiting/enrolling non-citizens for a
limited period is deleted.

102
Reply to the supplementary Questionnaire on Sashastra Seema Bal Bill, 2006
The Ministry of Home Affairs in their Action Taken Report on the 98th Report of the
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs on the Demands for Grants
(2003-04) had stated that reorganization of the SSB has not affected the service conditions of the
existing civilian personnel of the force.
(i) Question:–
Whether it has affected their promotional avenues? if so, to what extent and what
step Ministry has taken in that regard?
Answer:–
Consequent upon shifting of administrative control of SSB from Cabinet Secretariat to MHA
and change in the role of SSB to a Border Guarding Force, SSB has been reorganized as a Border
Guarding Force (BGF), which has led to the reorganization of the department for rationalization of
command structure.
Despite the decision to phase out the non-combatised cadres, they are being allowed
promotions within their own cadre as hitherto. Further, in order to ensure that the promotion of
non-combatised personnel do not suffer as a result of rationalization of the posts in SSB, the
Government has already decided to give them an opportunity to opt for combatisation.
(ii) Question:–
Whether mobility of personnel of SSB from organizational to Battalion and vice versa
was allowed before it was transferred from Cabinet Secretariat to MHA?
Answer:–
No. There was no such administrative/operational requirement.
(iii) Question:–
Whether any option of choosing combatised and non-combatised cadre was offered to
all personnel of SSB at the time of its re-organization. If so the details thereof.
Answer:–
No such option for choosing combatised and non-combatised cadre was offered to the
personnel of SSB Organization at the time of its reorganization. The personnel are continuing in
their respective streams with the entitlement of all the perks and allowances as hitherto including
the promotions within the respective cadres. Only the personnel of non-combatised streams can opt
for combatisation.
(iv) Question:–
Whether there had been any case of  junior combatised officer supervising a non-
combatised officer senior to him. If so, the details thereof and action taken in that regard.
Answer:–
There is no such case.
(v) Question
Whether the GoM on internal security and the Padamanabhaiah Committee had
categorically recommended for abolishing the civilian and executive cadres of SSB? If so,
what reasons were cited for their decisions? if not, what were the reasons for doing so.

103
Answer:–
Group of Ministers on the Internal Security and the Padmanabhaiah Committee had not
recommended the abolition of the civilian and executive cadres of SSB. However, in view of the
change in the role of SSB as a Border Guarding Force, it has been decided to make the fresh
recruitments in combatised categories only. The willing/eligible civilian personnel are also being
given an opportunity to opt for combatisation. Remaining civilian personnel will continue in their
respective grades and enjoy the existing perks/promotional avenues till they are phased out.
(vi) Question:–
A comparative chart of the cadre structures of Special Service Bureau before and
after restructuring may be supplied alongwith the maximum and minimum time taken by
the officers to get promotions? Please furnish the number and other details of the
personnel affected by new cadre structure.
Answer:–

104
Further total authorized post of I.G. in SSB are 08 out of which 03 are cadre post and
remaining have been allotted to IPS Officers.
(vii) Question:–
Whether the executive cadre officials of SSB were deployed on UN Mission before its
re-organization in 2001? if so, furnish reasons therefore.
Answer:–
Yes, the Executive Officials of SSB were being deployed on UN Mission before its re-
organization in 2001 because both the combatised and the non-combatised officials were
undergoing the same training/courses even upto 2003, both the officers of Executive cadre
(Organizational and Battalion cadre) have undergone similar training/courses and have similar
profiles. Non-combatised executive officers were sponsored for UN Mission as they fulfilled the
eligibility conditions. Now they are not being deployed in view of MHA order dated 4.2.2003 which
stipulates that only combatised officers will be nominated for UN Mission.

CHAPTER I 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
  
REVAMPING OF CIVIL DEFENCE 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS 
Para 8.3 
Civil Defence is an important and integral part of the defence of  the country. Particularly during
times of war Civil Defence Organi sation has a vital role in guard ing and protecting the people and
supporting civil administration. The Committee appreciates that National Disaster Management
Authority (NDMA) proposes to have relook at the sc heme of Revamping of Civil Defence and integrate
it into the National Disaster Management. The Committee agrees that Civil Defe nce is the right
organisation to be involved in Disa ster Management.  It however fe els that unduly long time has been
taken for revamping the Civil Defe nce System.  The Committee theref ore recommends that the issue
may be got cleared from the NDMA Committee and the Non-Plan Expenditure Committee and the final 
plan of action may be prepared for revamping the Civil Defence in th e shortest possible time schedule.
The Committee also recommends that funds for the scheme may be allocate d at RE 2006-07 stage an d 
the scheme may be implemented during the current financial year.  
  
ACTION TAKEN 
            The Ministry of Home Affairs accep ts the recommendation of the Committee to the extent that
there is a need to revamp the Civil Defence System at the earliest.  Once the NDMA Committee submits
its report/recommendations, appropriate proposals will be formulated and will be processed for approval
of the Government at the earliest.  However, to tal implementation of the scheme is proposed to be
completed in a period of 3 fiscal years. 
  
FURTHER ACTION TAKEN  
             
The matter is being pur sued with the NDMA Co mmittee for expediting its
report/recommendations so that th e scheme could be r ecast accordingly and processed for approval. 
Efforts will be made to obtain approval for the scheme and comm ence its implementation during the
current fiscal year.  
  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
            The Committee urges upon the Ministry to get the matter cleared from NDMA Committee
and start implementin g the scheme in ri ght earnest durin g the first quarter of the ensuin g
financial year.

MODERNISATION OF FIRE SERVICES 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS 
Para 9.2 
The Committee regrets that as in the case of th e scheme of Revamping of Civil Defence, the
scheme of Modernisation of Fire Se rvices too could not take off last year inspite of a provision of Rs.
134.26 crore in BE 2005-06. The Commit tee takes a serious view of th e fact that new schemes are 
initiated, allocations are made and they do not take  off due to procedural and administrative delays.
Although fire services in the c ountry are primarily the responsib ility of the States/Municipal
Committees/ Corporations, the services across th e country are abysmally below the International
Standards. The Committee desires that Modernisation of Fire Services which is a comprehensive scheme
should be equipped with modern  technology, gadgets and infrastr ucture.  The Committee while
expressing concern over delay of one year in implementing the scheme urges upon the Government to
get the scheme cleared in a definite time frame from NDM A and Planning Commission and make
necessary allocation at RE 2006-07 stage. The Committee also urges upon the Ministry to implement the 
scheme during the current fiscal year.              
  
ACTION TAKEN 
            The proposed scheme for Modernisation of Fire Services, formulated by the Ministry, is intended
as a one-time measure for financial assistance, in the form of gran ts in aid, to the States/UTs fo r
expansion, strengthening and modern ization of Fire Services upto a basic minimum level within a
definite time frame.  NDMA has seen and approve d the draft Scheme.  Under the proposed scheme, the
States/UTs are to contribute land for construction of  buildings for new Fire Stations and State Level
Training Institutes besides incu rring the recurring expenditure on payment of staff salary and
maintenance/up keep of buildings , vehicles and equipments afte r the scheme ge ts implemented. 
Provision of Rs. 134.26 crore was made  for the scheme on Non-Plan side  in BE 2005-06 in anticipation 
of final approval of the scheme so that implementation could immediately take  off.  However the
scheme could not be sanctioned during 2005-06.  The consent/confirmation of the States for discharging
their part of responsibility envisaged under the scheme is being obtained.  Once the consultation with the
States is completed, the Ministry will process the sc heme for approval of the competent authority at the
earliest.    
  
FURTHER ACTION TAKEN

women about their proactive approach in dealing with the cases of  atrocities committed against them.

with the practice of making this pr ovision out of the allocation made to Non Lapsable Central Pool o f

Rs. 100 crore is provided out of this Fund for BTC, the fund would get deplete d.  The Committee feels

MULTIPURPOSE NATIONAL IDENTITY CARDS SCHEME 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS 
Para 14.2 
The importance of the Mulit-purpose National Iden tity Card Scheme (MNI Cs) in a country like
India with thousands of kilometres of porous International Border and with the large pr esence of illegal
immigrants posing a grave threat to  the internal security, need not be overemphasized.  The Committee
is, however, disappointed at the pace of implementation of the pilot pr oject.  If the pilot project itself is
taking such a long time, preparation of MNICs for al l the citizens may take se veral more years.  The
Committee, therefore, urges upon the Government to accord high priori ty to the Scheme and accelerate
completion of the Pilot Project wi thin a specific time frame rather than dragging it endlessly.  The
Committee is confident that based on the experience gathered in the implementation of the Pilot Scheme
for the last two and a half years,  the Government would be in a position to evolve time bound action
plan for implementation of the scheme at the national level. 
  
ACTION TAKEN 
  
The pilot project was initiated in  November 2003 to be completed in one year.  However, actual
implementation has taken far longer due to difficulties encountered at almost each and every stage due
to following reasons: 
  
(a)
                this is the first time that such a project has been undertaken in the country. 
(b)               no precedent is available for such a comp lex project involving both processes an d
technology.   
(c)                unavailability of data entry operators in regional languages. 
(d)               difficulties in capturing of photographs and finger biometrics, specially for persons who
stay outside for employment, study etc. 
(e)                power was not available. Diesel Generator sets were to be arranged from far off places. 
(f)                 validation of individual data for correct spellings of names and other attributes. 
(g)                very cumbersome and tedious process of verifica tion of citizenship;  individuals were 
not found at their place of residence. 
(h)                weak document base for determ ining citizenship of individua ls in rural areas, specially
for agricultural labourers, landless labourers, married females etc.  
(i)                  unavailability of officials from State Government for this work. 
  
Following has been the physical and financial progress of the Project so far: 
  
(a)        Out of the tota l Budget of Rs. 19.89 crore allocated  during the financial year 2005-2006, 
total expenditure of Rs. 3.39 crore was incurred.  The ma jor expenditure would be on
identity (smart)cards which would be in curred after the cards are prepared and
distributed.  This is expected to be done in the current year i.e. 2006-2007. 
(b)        Steps are underway for completion of  the pilot projec t without delay.  The progress on
different items of work relating to Pilot Pr oject on Multi-purpose National identity Cards 
has been as follows:-

information  of each individual for preparation of population register – completed.
(ii)                Data entry in electronic format—completed.

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED
BY GOVERNMENT
NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR)
Recommendation (Para 7.1)
4.0    The Committee observes that NLCPR being a developmental corpus, it should be used for various development projects of the
region but is constrained to note that special packages are also met out of this fund. Any allocation from it for some other purpose is
neither desirable nor permissible. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should stop such practice and make separate
allocation for special packages.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
4.1    The matter was taken up with the Ministry of Finance who have supported the recommendation. Accordingly, the funds for the
Bodoland Territorial Council Area and for meeting the States’ share under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan would be found within the budgets of
Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of Human Resource Development without any additionality from the Centre and not from
NLCPR.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:
4.2    The Committee is satisfied with the action taken by the Ministry.
NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL (NEC)
Recommendation (Para 8.5)
5.0    The Committee notes with concern that the Tenth Plan Outlay for NEC has not been adhered to till 2006-07 even though it is the
terminal year of the plan. The final allocation made in each year put together leaves a gap of Rs. 988.5 crore. Had this amount been
allocated, all the projects could have been completed. The explanation of the Secretary, NEC that a host of projects are languishing from
scarcity of funds can be understood from the fact that the expenditure on the projects has been around hundred percent all the years. The
Committee fails to understand why the Planning Commission makes outlay for the Plan period and does not adhere to it while allocating
it every year. This is not the right approach, particularly in view of requirement of funds for the development of NER. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that the amount required for completion of the projects in the current financial year, which is also the
terminal year for Tenth Plan, may be made at RE stage.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
5.1    The recommendations have been noted and NEC would be advised to submit RE proposals in line with the recommendations.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:
5.2    The Committee notes that this is a critical area and calls upon the Ministry to communicate to it immediately the status of RE
proposals in relation to NEC.
Recommendation (Para 8.6)
6.0    The Committee is also given to understand that there is no proper monitoring mechanism to ensure quality and speedy execution of
the projects of NEC. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the monitoring mechanism may be strengthened to ensure quality and
speedy execution of the projects.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
6.1.0  The methods of Evaluation and Monitoring of NEC funded Schemes/Projects include the following:
               •      Preparation of Monthly Initiative.
               •      Preparation of Quarterly Progress Report (QPR).
               •      Financial Returns and Audit Reports.
               •      Intensive Inspection by NEC Officers.
               •      Quarterly Review by the Secretary.
               •      Periodical review of Schemes/Projects by the Steering Committee.
               •      Monthly performance review with Sectoral Heads.
               •      Monthly review with States on rotation basis.
               •      Obtaining photographs to assess progress.
               •      Concurrent Evaluation of ongoing Schemes/Projects suffering from implementation failure.

               •      Technical Evaluation of the construction of buildings.
               •      Establishment of Management Information System (MIS).

the Council more viable and relevant. A Quarterly Progress Report showing the physical and financial achievements in respect of each of
the NEC Schemes is prepared on a regular basis and circulated to all concerned. The Evaluation Advisory Committee of NEC constituted

Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
6.2     The Committee has noted that Evaluation Advisory Committee of NEC has recommended for evaluation-cum-impact study of 26
completed projects. The Committee desires to know the number of projects for which study has been completed and the details thereof.
ADVOCACY AND PUBLICITY:
Recommendation (Para 9.1)
7.0     The Committee appreciates the positive attitude of the States in coming up with proposals for capacity enhancement and hopes that
this approach would be maintained all through in implementing the schemes successfully. The Committee also notes that under the
Advocacy and Publicity, more than ninety five percent expenditure of the allocation has been made and the Ministry has also indicated
that several activities have been taken up at various places in the country. The Committee, however, feels that more needs to be done
under this scheme until the entire region is brought into the mainstream of the economy. More innovative programmes may be
undertaken and the Ministry of DoNER may approach the Ministry of Finance for higher allocation, if need be.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
Capacity Building:
7.1.0  The Ministry has ongoing arrangements with National/Regional institutes and centres of excellence, which are being continued this
year as well. In addition, as desired by the Parliamentary Standing Committee, the Ministry is venturing into newer areas of capacity
building. One of such initiatives is in ‘aviation sector’. It is planned to train youth from the North Eastern States as commercial pilots and
aircraft maintenance engineers so as to overcome the shortage of aviation staff willing to serve in the NER and thereby improve
connectivity.
Advocacy and Publicity:
7.1.1  This year the Ministry is proposing to hold exhibitions on regional basis to showcase NE products and strengths in major cities like
New Delhi, Chennai, Bangalore and Hyderabad. An exhibition-cum-buyer-seller meet was held in Mumbai in collaboration with CII. An
elaborate programme to showcase the strength of the region through electronic media is underway.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:
7.2     The Committee notes the action proposed to be taken by the Ministry to train the youth of the NE States as commercial pilot and
aircraft maintenance engineers. This needs to be pursued immediately particularly in view of the scarcity of pilots in the country.
EXTERNALLY AIDED PROJECTS (EAPs)
Recommendations (Para 10.2)
8.0     The externally aided projects, if implemented in the right earnest, would go a long way in improving the infrastructure in the North
East. The final report on Phase-I of the NE Urban Development Project may be processed and examined at the earliest and the project
proposals may be prepared soon. The Ministry should make all efforts to ensure that Phase-I goes through this year. As regards the NE
State Road Project, the Committee desires that the submission of draft Report be completed at the earliest and efforts be made to see that
the project takes off this year. The study of NE Trade and Investment Creation Initiative may be got competed at the earliest so that other
processes could be taken up. In regard to the World Bank study on natural resources, water and environment nexus for development and
growth, efforts may be made to complete the study on all aspects positively in this financial year.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
8.1.0  The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is providing Project Preparatory Technical Assistance (PPTA) in two phases. During Phase-
I, five capital cities viz. Agartala, Aizaw, Kohima, Shillong and Gangtok have been taken up. Phase-II will cover four cities viz.,
Guwahati, Dibrugarh, Imphal and Itanagar. The ADB Consultants have submitted draft Report for Phase-I cities Action is being initiated
by Ministry of DoNER/State Governments in the light of ADB’s observations in the Aide-Memoire.
8.1.1  As regards the North-Eastern State Roads Projects (NESRP), the final Report has since been submitted by the ADB Consultants.

Requisite consultations have taken place with all concerned on  29th June and 14th July, 2006.
8.1.2  The key issue for consideration at this stage is the financing pattern. During 2005-06, the Ministry of Finance had taken a policy
decision to transfer external assistance to States on ‘back-to-back basis’. Most NE States have an extremely narrow resource base and are
not in a position to take the external assistance on ‘back-to-back basis’. The restoration of earlier prevailing financing pattern of 90:10 is
awaiting decision of the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance.
8.1.3  The ADB Consultants on “NE States Trade and Investment Creation Initiative” Project have submitted their draft final Report. It
was discussed with the eight NE State Governments and other stakeholders in a Regional workshop held at Guwahati on 13th July, 2006.
8.1.4  The Strategy Report prepared by the World Bank on “Natural Resources, Water and Environment Nexus for Development and
Growth in North East India” was discussed in a Consultation Workshop held at New Delhi from 26-27 June, 2006. Ministry of
Development of North-Eastern Region had extended financial assistance to the eight NE States for organizing State Level Workshops
during April-June, 2006. The objective was to discuss the draft Report in a transparent manner and provide an opportunity to all
interested stakeholders to give their considered inputs.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:
8.2    The Committee having noted the responses of the Ministry of DoNER recommends that the Ministry of Finance may take prompt
decision on restoration of earlier prevailing financing pattern of Externally Aided Projects.
VISION NER: 2020
Recommendations (Para 11.2)
9.0    The Committee is of the view that the Vision Document being a 15 year perspective  plan for integrated and holistic development of
NER through the process of participatory planning, must provide for concerted efforts to tap the potential and strengths of the region,
remove weaknesses and it should be prepared in consultation with all the stakeholders. Sports and textiles are two sectors that have
tremendous potential of growth in the NE region. Prowess of sportspersons of the region has been manifested at various national and
international levels. The need is for providing the ideal environment and infrastructure for allowing this talent to grow. Textiles are one
of the most important thrust areas not only to earn foreign exchange but also to provide employment to a large number of people
particularly to the rural artisans. Thus sports and textiles are two major strengths of the region and need to be given special thrust in the
Document. The Committee also recommends that establishment of a national level sports school and an institute like National Institute of
Fashion Technology in NER should be included in the Vision Document 2020.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
9.1    The recommendations have been noted and are being incorporated in the Vision 2020 Document which is in an advanced stage of
completion.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:
9.2    The Committee notes the reply and would like to be informed immediately of the present status of Vision Document: 2020.
NATIONAL BAMBOO MISSION
Recommendations (Para 15.1)
10.0  The Committee agrees that in view of the conducive  climatic condition and heavy rainfall, the Bamboo Mission would boost the
plantation of bamboo in the region, which would certainly help the sagging economy of NE States. The Committee wants early
implementation of National Bamboo Mission in the region so that the Ministry of DoNER and NEC could accelerate projects under the
Mission. The Ministry and NEC may, therefore, take up the matter with the Ministry of Agriculture for early approval of the Mission.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
10.1  Department of Agriculture and Cooperation has informed that the proposed Scheme of Bamboo Mission has been referred to a
Group of Ministers (GoM) by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) Further action in the matter will be taken after the
Report of the GoM.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
10.2  The Committee while noting the reply would like to be informed of the latest position in the matter. The Committee suggests that
the Ministry of DoNER may expedite the follow-up action for implementation of the National Bamboo Mission.

CHAPTER- II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN
ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR)
Recommendation (Para 7.7)
11.0   The Committee does not agree with the Ministry of Finance of its plan to enable the NE States to raise loans from the open market.
The Committee is of the firm view that these States would not be able to raise loans from the market. The prevailing atmosphere in the
NE region too is not conducive for private investment. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier observation that non-budgeting of
loan component of Central assistance to States is not a viable proposition for the special category States of NER and recommends that the
budgeting of loan component may be provided.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
11.1   The matter was taken up with the Ministry of Finance. They have informed that the decision not to provide budgetary support for
loan component has been taken on the recommendations of the Twelfth Finance Commission and now all Central Assistance to the State
Plan is released by the Centre in the form of grants only and the States have been advised to raise borrowings directly from the market.
Ministry of Finance has pointed out that during 2005-06, no North Eastern State has faced any difficulty in raising the borrowings
directly from the market and during that period an amount of Rs. 1900.13 crore has been raised by them without any difficulty. In view
thereof, Ministry of Finance is of the view that it may not be prudent to provide the budgeting of loan component of Plan Assistance in
the Budget.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
11.2   The Committee is of the view that NE States because of their backwardness need special treatment. The Secretary, DoNER and
Secretary, NEC submitted before the Committee at the time of considering Demands for Grants for 2006-07 that all the NE States have
requested for budgeting of ten percent of loan component. In view of this, the stand taken by the Ministry of Finance is not convincing.
The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier observation and recommends that the loan component of Central Assistance to NE States
may also be budgeted as it used to be earlier.
CIVIL AVIATION IN NER
Recommendations (Para 12.6)
12.0   The Committee appreciates the problem involved in regard to the demand for engaging pilots and engineers from the private sector.
However, the problem of air connectivity in the North-Eastern Region cannot be ignored just because of this factor As a short-term
measure, the Government may take up the matter with the Indian Air Force to provide some Air Force pilots and engineers until a
permanent arrangement is made. For solving the problem on a long-term basis, the Ministry may discuss the issue of setting up a Pilot
Training Institute at Lilabari with Ministry of Civil Aviation at the earliest. Necessary allocation may also be made for starting the
Institute at the Revised Estimate stage. The Government may also include this in the ‘Vision Document 2020’
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
12.1.0  Dr. (Mrs.) I.K. Barthakur  had chaired an inter-ministerial meeting on 23.12.2005 to discuss the issue of providing improved air-
connectivity. The Alliance Air had expressed their inability to make Guwahati airport as the hub for operating the four ATR Aircrafts due
to shortage of pilots and technicians. However, it was assured that efforts would be made to recruit expatriate pilots for operating the
ATR aircraft.
12.1.1  Secretary, DoNER held a meeting on 16.03.2006 to review the MoU signed between ihe North Eastern Council and Alliance Air
for improving air connectivity in the NE Region. The Alliance Air was advised to take immediate steps to improve air connectivity in the
region The issue of shortage of pilots was also highlighted. Alliance Air was requested to base at least one ATR at Lokpriya  Gopinath
Bordoloi (LGB) airport, Guwahati and utilize it for effecting improved air connectivity.
12.1.2  Ministry of Defence has been requested to consider the recommendation of the Standing Committee to provide some IAF pilots
and engineers. The Ministry of Civil Aviation has been simultaneously requested to consider setting up of a Pilot Training Centre at
Lilabari.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
12.2   The Committee is not satisfied with the responses of the Ministry of DoNER. It notes that the approach of that Ministry for
improving air connectivity has been confined merely to making couple of requests and no road map has been prepared for achieving the
targets. The Committee would appreciate if Ministry of DoNER could apprise it of the latest position of action taken on each
recommendation. It would like to impress upon the Ministry to vigorously pursue the various issues so that decisions are taken thereon
within a reasonable period of time.

13.0   The Committee is dismayed at the extraordinary delay in the commencement of work on the project “Ropeway at Tawang in
Arunachal Pradesh” inaugurated by the President of India. Such delays and procrastination breeds resentment amongst the people of the
region against the administration. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Government to seek early sanction for the project and
complete the same in the shortest possible time frame.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
13.1   The Project “Construction of Ropeway from Tawang Monastery to Ani Gompa” in Arunachal Pradesh was recommended for
sanction at an estimated cost of Rs. 330.89 lakh by the NLCPR Committee in its 40th meeting held on 28.03.2006. The State Government
was requested on 17.05.2006 to submit the work plan and requirement of funds under first installment for release of funds. They have not
submitted as yet the work plan and are being reminded.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
13.2   The Committee expresses its deep concern over the inordinate delay in the commencement of the construction of ropeway from
Tawang Monastery to Ani Gompa due to the nonchalant attitude of the authorities and lack of coordination between Central and State
Governments. The Committee directs the Ministry to expedite the project and submit the work plan so that the funds could be released
and the long pending project may see the light of the day. The Ministry should also help the State Government either by itself or through
NEC in preparing the work plan for the project, if necessary required funds and technical assistance be released to the State Government.

CHAPTER-III
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT ARE STILL AWAITED
NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR):
Recommendation (Para 7.4)
14.0   The Committee finds that very important Ministries/Departments from the point of view of NER such as Ministries/Departments of
Science and Technology, Biotechnology and Space are in the list of exempted Ministries/Departments. These Ministries/Departments can
play an important role in the development of NER. Keeping in view the forest cover of the region, the bio-diversity development can be
given a boost through the involvement of Ministry of Science and Technology and Department of Biotechnology. Likewise, the
Department of Space, which has given matching contribution along with NEC for development of North Eastern Space Application
Centre (NESAC), Shillong, can also contribute significantly for the development of NER. These exempted Ministries/Departments
should be reviewed by the Government and considered for the purpose of spending ten per cent of their GBS for the development of
NER. The Committee hopes that the assurance given by the Secretary would be fulfilled at the earliest.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
14.1   The matter is under processing.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
14.2   The Committee urges upon the Ministry to expedite the follow-up action to include the Ministries/ Departments of Science and
Technology, Biotechnology and Space in the list of Ministries/Departments which mandatorily contribute ten per cent of their Grant
Budgetary Support for the development of NE Region, as assured by the Secretary, DoNER. The Committee may be apprised of the
action taken thereon.
CIVIL AVIATION IN NER
Recommendation (Para 12.3)
15.0   The Committee is not happy with the way the issue of air connectivity in the North Eastern Region has been handled, particularly
by the Planning Commission. It is surprising that the Planning Commission has taken more than five years to process the proposals for
airports at Passighat and Teju in Arunachal Pradesh and even after five years, no decision has been taken and ‘in-principle’ approval has
not been given. The Committee observes that such delays ate one of the factors for which the North-Eastern Region has remained
backward. The real potential and the strengths available in the region have not been properly tapped and air connectivity is no exception
to this. Such casual approach and bureaucratic delays only create heart burning amongst the people of the region. When the Committee
visited North East early this year, several people who met it sought to know as to how long they have to wait for implementation of these
projects. The Committee takes strong note of this nonchalant approach and recommends that the Planning Commission should clear the
projects without further delay to enable the Ministry of Civil Aviation and the State Government to implement the projects at the earliest.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
15.1   Tezu  and Pasighat airports in Arunachal  Pradesh were included in the 10th Plan of NEC. The Planning Commission has not yet
accorded ‘in principle’ approval to the proposals. Secretary, DoNER addressed a D.O. letter to the Sr. Consultant, Planning Commission
on 30.03.2006 requesting for expediting the ‘in principle’ approval. The recommendation of the Standing Committee has also been
conveyed to the Planning Commission and their comments invited. A reply is awaited.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
15.2   The Committee takes a serious view of the lack of response of the Planning Commission in the matter. Such indifference and
indecisiveness belie the pronouncements of the Government on improving the air connectivity in the NER. The Committee would like the
Ministry of DoNER to again pursue the matter with the Planning Commission and apprise it of the decisions taken on its
observations/recommendations before it takes up scrutiny of the Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the year 2007-2008.
HEALTH CARE IN NER
Recommendations (Para 13.2)
16.0   The Committee finds it quite unusual that even after fifty-nine years of independence there are States which do not have even one
medical college and that the demand for the same is quite justified. Setting up of a medical college, besides providing trained medical
graduates, would also bring with it better medical facilities and health infrastructure. The States without medical colleges would all the
more require such facilities besides getting medical graduates. The Committee strongly recommends that at least one medical college in
each of the States of Arunachal  Pradesh, Mizoram  and Nagaland may be set up. This should be considered on priority basis and
allocation may be made at RE stage. This may also be included in the Vision Document 2020.
Action Taken/Proposed to be Taken
16.1   The matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The reply is awaited.
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
